title: Toward a Quantum Information Foundation for Neutron Scattering
abstract: Neutron scattering is a central probe of quantum materials, yet what quantum information can, in principle, be extracted from a scattering experiment remains unclear. Here we formulate neutron scattering as a quantum measurement, with the scattering amplitudes acting as Kraus operators on the material state. This provides a unified description of conventional intensity, coherent scattering, interferometric measurements, and entanglement witnesses, including those based on quantum Fisher information. We then ask how far this connection can be extended to nonlinear properties of a quantum state. For two independently prepared samples, we derive the general structure of probe-mediated measurement probabilities and show that, for spin-projection-conserving dynamics, low-order scattering cannot resolve certain many-body coherences required to determine purity. Conversely, an idealized single-spin protocol shows how probe-mediated exchange can access purity when the appropriate two-copy operation is realized. Our results establish a quantum-information description of neutron scattering and delineate the information accessible through conventional and interferometric measurements.

title: The compact gas-dynamic ion-beam extractor/buncher module for the cryogenic stopping cells at FAIR
abstract: Abstract The original compact gas-dynamic ion-beam extractor/buncher module is proposed here as a new instrument for low-energy ion-beam manipulation. In order to enhance the quality of pulsed cold ion beams extracted from the two cryogenic stopping cells at FAIR (i.e., the one currently used in the FRS and the one under development for the Super-FRS at FAIR), it is hereby proposed that this module be utilised as a substitute for the extensively employed linear radiofrequency quadrupole (RFQ) technique. The proposed apparatus facilitates the extraction and fast bunching of approximately 100% ions into a vacuum by means of a short stack of thin cylindrical electrodes positioned on the axis behind the extraction RF carpet nozzle. The implementation of the proposal will enable the achievement of low emittance values for short-pulsed ion beams in a wide mass range, as demonstrated by detailed gas-dynamic and ion trajectory Monte Carlo simulations. The results of these simulations are presented and discussed.

title: Interacting Boson System at Finite Temperatures: The treatment of the lattice QCD results
abstract: We study an interacting relativistic system of charged bosons at finite temperature and fixed isospin density within a thermodynamically consistent mean-field approach. The interaction is represented by repulsive phi-4 and phi-6 self-interactions, which generate a density-dependent effective mass of the bosonic quasiparticles. We formulate the thermodynamics in the Extended Canonical Ensemble, obtained from the grand canonical description by a Legendre transformation from the isospin chemical potential to the conserved isospin density. In the condensed phase the chemical potential is constrained by the Bose-condensation condition and is therefore determined self-consistently through the effective mass. We apply the formalism to a pion-like system at finite isospin and clarify the relation between the isospin chemical-potential conventions used for pion and quark degrees of freedom. Using the convention adopted in lattice-QCD calculations, we compare the pressure, isospin density, energy density, and trace anomaly with lattice results at T=120 MeV. With one constant fitted to the lattice pressure, each model reproduces the lattice isospin density, energy density, and trace anomaly. Both the phi-4 and phi-6 models reproduce the main features of the lattice data, with the phi-6 interaction providing the better description. The Extended Canonical Ensemble provides a convenient framework for treating interacting particle-antiparticle systems across the transition to the Bose-condensed phase.

title: From lattice QCD thermodynamics to an effective quasiparticle description of gluonic matter at finite temperature
abstract: We develop a lattice-constrained quasiparticle description of pure SU(3) Yang--Mills matter at finite temperature. The temperature-dependent effective gluon quasiparticle mass is determined from the lattice entropy density over $0.70\leq T/T_c\leq5$. It is interpreted as an effective thermal parameter encoding medium modifications of gluonic excitations, rather than as a physical gluon mass. With this mass fixed, we reconstruct the background contribution required for thermodynamic consistency, using a single pressure-normalization condition. The resulting pressure, energy density, entropy density, interaction measure, and squared speed of sound are then compared with available lattice results. Near $T_c$, the rapid variation of the effective mass is accompanied by a pronounced maximum in the interaction measure at $T/T_c\simeq1.09$, a strong suppression of the squared speed of sound, and a maximum in the background contribution. These correlated features characterize the substantial departure from conformal behavior in the transition region. At higher temperatures, the interaction measure decreases and the squared speed of sound approaches the conformal limit. We also examine the energy-per-excitation ratio $E/n_g$, which has a minimum of approximately $964~\mathrm{MeV}$ at $T/T_c\simeq1.21$. This ratio provides a measure of the excitation scale within the quasiparticle description. Overall, our results show how lattice thermodynamics can be mapped onto an effective gluonic excitation spectrum while maintaining thermodynamic consistency.

title: Development of a positron imaging unit for advanced plant research
abstract: Abstract Positron-emitting tracer imaging systems (PETIS) apply the principles of positron emission tomography to plant research, enabling non-destructive, real-time visualization of substance distribution in living plants. However, the conventional PETIS instruments using bismuth germanate (BGO) scintillator arrays and position-sensitive photomultiplier tubes have limited spatial resolution 1.6–2.1 mm full width at half maximum (FWHM), and the relatively long decay time of BGO restricts the coincidence timing resolution (CTR) and count-rate performance. In addition, the thickness of the scintillator array can introduce parallax errors due to depth-of-interaction ambiguity. To enable submillimeter-scale imaging of fine structures like leaf veins, we developed a compact, high-resolution prototype PETIS unit tailored for thin plant organs. The prototype features two face-to-face detector modules separated by 2 cm. Each module consists of a finely segmented cerium-doped gadolinium aluminium gallium garnet scintillator array (1 × 1 × 1 and 1.5 × 1.5 × 1 mm 3 crystals), a 1-mm light guide, an 8 × 8 silicon photomultiplier array, and a TOFPET2 application-specific integrated circuit. The 1-mm-thick scintillator design drastically reduces depth-of-interaction parallax errors while optimizing count-rate capability. The performance was evaluated using a 22 Na point source. The system achieved 511 keV energy resolutions of 11–13 % FWHM. Reconstructed images demonstrated spatial resolutions of 1.1–1.2 mm FWHM, significantly outperforming the conventional PETIS instruments. The CTR reached 773 ± 16 ps with an effective coincidence detection efficiency of 6.54 × 10 -5 . These fundamental performance results demonstrate the strong potential of the compact unit for localized, high-resolution plant transport studies.

title: Development and characterization of a wingless ICPC HPGe detector with thin amorphous-Ge contacts
abstract: Abstract High-purity germanium (HPGe) detectors with thin amorphous-germanium (a-Ge) contacts can provide bipolar charge blocking and surface passivation while minimizing contact-related inactive thickness. We report the fabrication and characterization of a p-type inverted coaxial point-contact (ICPC) HPGe detector using thin a-Ge contacts in a wingless geometry that avoids the protective wing structure used in our previous prototype. The detector was fabricated from a USD-grown, zone-refined HPGe crystal and has a mass of 20.0 g. With the temperature controller set to 77 K, the detector exhibited picoampere-scale leakage current and an operational depletion voltage of approximately 440 V. A representative monitored temperature of approximately 76.3 K was recorded during detector characterization. Gamma-ray spectroscopy yielded energy resolutions of 1.8 keV FWHM at 59.5 keV and 3.2 keV FWHM at 662 keV. The calibrated charge-injection method gave a pulser-derived effective capacitance of 0.496 pF, compared with the simulated intrinsic detector capacitance of 0.488 pF obtained using SolidStateDetectors.jl . With a 241 Am source positioned inside the detector bore, the detector showed a source-correlated excess current and a broad degraded-alpha continuum centered near 3558 keV, demonstrating sensitivity to near-surface interactions. Because the source encapsulation, intervening materials, and near-surface charge-collection response were not independently characterized, the continuum is not used to infer a unique dead-layer thickness or energy-loss mechanism. The principal result is successful fabrication and stable sub-pF operation of a 20-g wingless thin-contact ICPC prototype.

title: Systematical examination of the B 4 / 2 anomaly as a signature of enhanced triaxiality at the border of shape-coexistence regions
abstract: The ${B}_{4/2}$ ratio of reduced transition strengths between the low-lying yrast states is systematically examined in even-even as well as in odd-$A$ nuclei in the $28\ensuremath{\le}Z\ensuremath{\le}92$ region. In all standard collective models in which the structure evolves from a vibrational to an axially deformed idealized case, this ratio is always greater than unity. By examining available experimental data, this study shows that not all isotopes in the nuclear chart exhibit this characteristic. A thorough search for this anomalous behavior revealed that 41 nuclei have a ratio ${B}_{4/2}<$ 1, with 27 isotopes having upper uncertainties that do not exceed unity. While this phenomenon has remained a mystery for a long time, in recent years it has been speculated that triaxiality could be responsible for this behavior. In this paper, the role of triaxiality is analyzed for all these nuclei with the rigid triaxial rotor and the proxy-SU(3) theoretical models. We find that triaxiality is not the only ingredient necessary for a value ${B}_{4/2}<1$ , but the appearance of these regions is strongly correlated with the border of a shape-coexistence region, along with the presence of enhanced triaxiality.

title: Large Offsets of Double-neutron-star Mergers: Degeneracies and Implications for Host Associations
abstract: Abstract The projected offset of a gamma-ray burst (GRB) from its host galaxy is an important diagnostic of its physical origin, where the host associations are usually evaluated through chance-coincidence probabilities. However, as shown by observations, the host associations given by this approach may be ambiguous in some cases. In this work, we revisit the modelling of the offsets of double-neutron-star (DNS) mergers with controlled numerical experiments using Monte Carlo simulations. To isolate the dynamical effects of the second supernova (SN) from uncertainties in the upstream binary evolution, we parametrize the direct progenitor of DNSs and integrate the post-SN trajectories in galactic potentials using galpy . Complementary to previous population synthesis calculations, our Monte Carlo tool, GRB-offset , provides a lightweight framework to identify sensitivities and expose degeneracies in offset modelling. With GRB-offset , we have investigated the following physical ingredients: SN physics (ejected mass and kick velocity), galactic potential (potential shape, galaxy virial mass), DNS birth location, star formation history, and redshift. The offset distributions given by our reference Monte Carlo simulation peak at around 30 and 1000 kpc for the DNSs bound to and unbound from the host galaxy, which sensitively depends on the considered physical ingredients. A given offset can arise from various combinations of these ingredients, introducing substantial degeneracies when interpreting observed offsets. Therefore, an observed offset alone can hardly constrain the properties of the DNS progenitor and of the host galaxies.

title: Spurious center-of-mass mode as an $S$-matrix pole within the Jost-random-phase approximation
abstract: Within the Jost-random-phase approximation (Jost-RPA), the spurious center-of-mass mode is a zero of the Jost determinant and hence a pole of the $S$ matrix. A zero at zero excitation energy $E$, whether from self-consistency or from a calibration of the residual interaction, is a pole of exactly second order when it has a single independent solution, every unoccupied bound orbital lies above the holes, and each hole is paired with every allowed partial wave; the order follows from the position of the zero, not from self-consistency. The state of this double pole, given by the Autonne-Takagi factorization of its $E^{-2}$ coefficient, is the zero-energy solution normalized by its inertia. In a self-consistent model of one energy density of the neutron and proton densities, every physical $S$-matrix element continued to $E=0$ carries the $E^{-2}$ term, contrary to an earlier conclusion. Subtracting the mode's principal part from the response changes the strength at real $E\neq0$ only through the smoothing and, in such a model, coincides with the projection of the ideal spurious state. In uncalibrated Woods-Saxon models of $^{16}$O and $^{208}$Pb the mode is a pair of poles on the imaginary axis.

title: QCD phase structure at high baryon density
abstract: Heavy-ion collisions provide unique access to the properties of QCD matter over a broad range of temperatures and baryon densities. We review recent progress in constraining the high-density phase structure of QCD, with particular emphasis on the microscopic inputs required for reliable transport modeling. We discuss cluster production, strange-particle interactions, collision dynamics at few-GeV energies, and the isospin dependence of the nuclear interaction, together with their impact on the interpretation of flow, yields, fluctuations, and possible critical signatures.

title: Chromatic Calorimetry -- A Novel Approach to Validate Energy Resolution and Particle Discrimination
abstract: Chromatic calorimetry (CCAL) analyses particle detection by utilizing scintillators with distinct emission wavelengths to measure the longitudinal energy deposition of particle showers in high-energy physics, improving particle identification (PID) and energy resolution. By stacking scintillators in order of decreasing emission wavelength, CCAL enables layer-specific energy measurements, analyzed via amplitude fractions ($f_i = A_i / \sum_j A_j$) and center of gravity ($\langle z_{\text{cog}} \rangle = \sum_i z_i E_i / \sum_i E_i$). This thesis presents results from two CERN Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) experiments conducted in 2023 and 2024, complemented by GEANT4 simulations of a quantum dot (QD)-based CCAL design, to validate its potential for future colliders such as the Future Circular Collider (FCC).

title: CMS ECAL Phase-2 upgrade: characterisation and stability analysis of a three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system
abstract: As part of the High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider, the front-end electronics of the Compact Muon Solenoid electromagnetic calorimeter barrel are being replaced. A three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system supplies the upgraded electronics. As the cascade dynamics require characterisation to ensure stable operation, interactions between the three converter stages are assessed at their two interfaces using the Nyquist criterion. A validated shunt-injection setup using a Bode 100 frequency-response analyser provides in-situ impedance measurements under load to assess the accuracy of the averaged converter models. Results show that both interfaces are stable over the evaluated configurations, with modelled minimum distances to the critical point of 0.76 and 0.79, respectively. A turn-on study identifies capacitor charging at Stage 3 as the main cause of inrush currents triggering Stage 2 overcurrent protection. Two Stage 3 board variants stagger converter enables within and between boards, keeping the measured two-tower current below 5 A, within the 8.0 A protection threshold.

title: Tritium breeding lifetime assessment of a ceramic-based blanket in a fusion tokamak device
abstract: Abstract Achieving tritium self-sufficiency is a critical requirement for the viability of future fusion power plants. Here, a comprehensive assessment of the operational lifetimes of ceramic breeder materials under neutron irradiation within a tokamak environment is resented, focusing on the evolution of the tritium breeding ratio (TBR) over reactor-relevant timescales. This is defined here as the operational timeframe at which the TBR is maintained above a critical threshold of ≈1.10. Using the depletion capabilities within the OpenMC neutronics code, both conventional ceramic breeders (Li2TiO3, Li4SiO4, and advanced ceramic breeder – ACB) and emerging hybrid breeder-multiplier ceramics (Li8PbO6, Li2Be2O3) are assessed for operational lifetime strategies. Initial optimisation identifies breeder-to-multiplier volumetric ratios that maximise TBR at time zero, followed by time-dependent simulations to quantify TBR degradation due to lithium depletion during service. It is shown that while higher initial multiplier fractions enhance TBR, they also accelerate lithium depletion, reducing blanket lifetime. Conversely, hybrid ceramics with intrinsic neutron multiplication show reduced sensitivity to additional multipliers. A novel layer-wise optimisation approach, varying breeder and multiplier distributions radially and poloidally, is shown to extend blanket lifetimes and maintain TBR above the critical threshold for longer periods demonstrating lifetime limitations may be elsewhere within the breeder blanket. Verification against FISPACT-II confirms the accuracy of the OpenMC depletion methodology utilised. The results highlight the importance of spatially optimised material distributions and lithium inventory management in maximising breeder blanket longevity. This work provides robust framework for the design of next-generation solid breeder blankets, offering practical strategies to minimise replacement frequency and support sustainable fusion energy.

title: Performance and damage mechanisms of dispersion-strengthened tungsten under H-mode plasma in DIII-D
abstract: Abstract Dispersion strengthened tungsten (DSW) alloys are promising materials for plasma facing components, displaying improved mechanical properties and microstructure stability compared to pure tungsten. In this work, the performance of DSW reinforced with 1 wt% transition-metal carbide (TaC, TiC, or ZrC) has been examined under H-mode plasma in the DIII-D tokamak. DSW samples were mounted both flush with the divertor floor and at a 10° angle towards the incoming plasma fluxes to further increase the heat and particle loading. To simulate the impact of prolonged tokamak operation, similar plasma exposures were repeated on two additional sets of DSW samples: one set pre-implanted with 10 22 m -2 helium, and another set heated in-situ to an additional 500°C. Flush mounted samples exhibited good surface stability, with no evidence of melting or cracking regardless of composition or treatment. Carbon redeposition was observed on most samples, likely due to the graphite environment of DIII-D. Under coupled thermal loading and helium implantation, surface nanostructuring developed in some DSW samples; however, DSW containing tantalum dispersion phases showed strong resistance to such surface modification. In contrast, obvious surface melting was observed on 10° angled samples containing TaC and ZrC dispersoids, likely associated with dispersoid oxidation during fabrication, which reduced thermal conductivity and promoted elevated surface temperatures during plasma exposure. The grain morphology of DSW containing TiC remained largely unchanged, although near-surface dispersoids on the angled TiC sample were missing after plasma exposure. The loss is associated with oxidation of the dispersoids during fabrication, followed by sublimation during plasma exposure. Through systematic comparison of DSW performance under H-mode plasma conditions, this study identifies key degradation mechanisms and highlights strategies to improve the performance of DSW as plasma facing materials.

title: Measurement, modeling, and correction of decapolar Hamiltonian terms in the LHC
abstract: Understanding and mitigating high-order nonlinearities is essential for ensuring long-term beam storage in high-energy colliders. The stability of particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is indeed strongly influenced by nonlinear effects, particularly at injection energy where the beam occupies a large fraction of the vacuum chamber. Among these effects, third-order chromaticity, primarily driven by decapolar fields, limits dynamic aperture and beam lifetime. Despite corrections based on magnetic measurements and model predictions, a discrepancy remains between the measured and expected third-order chromaticity, indicating the presence of residual decapolar components. In this study, the decapolar fields in the LHC at injection energy are investigated and their impact on beam dynamics assessed. Chromatic amplitude detuning and decapolar resonance driving terms are directly measured for the first time, using forced oscillations driven by an ac dipole. These measurements provide new insights into the source and impact of decapolar fields in the LHC and indicate that refined correction strategies could enhance beam lifetime, particularly for high-brightness operation in future runs.

title: Machine-learned particle flow as a foundation model for collider physics
abstract: The workflow from particle collision to physics analysis passes through a series of reconstruction steps that are traditionally modular and disconnected, with no shared representation linking low-level detector data to high-level analysis tasks. We show that casting event reconstruction as a machine learning problem naturally produces such a shared representation. We repurpose a machine learning model trained for particle-flow reconstruction (MLPF) to perform three distinct analysis tasks: jet flavor identification, jet energy regression, and missing momentum regression. By appending the per-particle latent representations learned during reconstruction as additional input features, we substantially improve over baselines that use conventional particle-level features alone. We further demonstrate that a single linear layer trained using only the latent representations achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art baseline architectures, and outperforms the baseline for missing momentum regression with approximately 35 times fewer parameters. These results demonstrate that the latent representations learned during reconstruction encode essential physics information needed for downstream analysis, establishing MLPF as a foundation model and offering a concrete step toward an end-to-end pipeline from detector data to physics analysis.

title: Core reduction for increasing neutron flux and radioisotope production in the IEA-R1 research reactor
abstract: This work aims to present and analyze a new reactor core configuration for the IEA-R1 reactor core with the objective of enhancing its neutron irradiation capabilities. The reactor was modeled using the KENO-VI module from the SCALE Code System, provided by ORNL. Results have shown that implementing a near-cylindrical configuration with 20 fuel elements in the IEA-R1 core could substantially increase neutron flux, particularly in the center irradiation positions such as the EIBe (Beryllium Irradiated Element). After comparing various configurations, we conducted a brief analysis of the proposed core configuration's potential to produce 177Lu, resulting in a 34% increase in the specific activity of 177Lu considering a fuel power cycle around 21 days.

title: CMS ECAL VFE Production Qualification
abstract: Upgrading the CMS ECAL barrel for the HL-LHC requires replacement of all on-detector electronics, including 12240 Very-Front-End (VFE) cards employing CATIA and LiTE-DTU ASICs for amplification and digitisation of signals from ECAL's 61200 lead-tungstate crystals. All production VFEs undergo the same qualification procedure: functional testing, environmental stress screening, and calibration. We have received and functionally tested 13596 unique VFEs; two never passed our test criteria. Results for other VFEs are uniform and within expectations, demonstrating the excellent quality of the cards. Key metrics, such as a gain ratio of $10.21 \pm 0.07$ and power consumption of $1.805 \pm 0.013~\mathrm{W}$, demonstrate high consistency across the batch.

title: Toward high-performance tracking simulation of long-range resistive-wall driven transverse coupled-bunch instabilities
abstract: The long-range transverse resistive-wall (RW) wakefield is a key driver of transverse coupled-bunch instabilities in high-current storage rings. Simulating these instabilities accurately is typically time-consuming, because conventional time-domain tracking codes such as store the turn-by-turn bunch-centroid history and perform discrete convolutions with the wakefield, which poses a bottleneck for long-term tracking. To overcome this limitation, this work reformulates the long-range RW wakefield calculation, converting the explicit history-dependent convolution into a recursive update by representing the wakefield as a sum-of-exponential functions. This approach avoids storing the bunch-centroid history and is well suited to parallel graphics-processing-unit architectures; it has been implemented in the tracking code . Benchmark tests, using parameters of the Hefei Advanced Light Facility (HALF), show that with the proposed method maintains high accuracy in the growth rate while achieving a speedup of at least 2 orders of magnitude over . Leveraging this computational efficiency, we conduct a systematic study of RW instabilities for HALF, with particular focus on the interplay among filling pattern, chromaticity, and harmonic-cavity bunch lengthening.

title: Suppression of transient beam-loading effects in storage rings via main-cavity power source feedforward scheme
abstract: Dual-frequency radio-frequency systems are widely deployed in high-brightness synchrotron radiation light sources to achieve electron bunch lengthening. However, the transient beam-loading (TBL) effect induced by bunch gaps causes significant synchronous phase shifts and severely compromises bunch-lengthening performance. To address this, we propose an active compensation scheme that suppresses voltage fluctuations in both the main and harmonic cavities by modulating only the driving voltage of the main cavity via a feedforward approach. To elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms, we establish a gap-induced linear decomposition analytical model, which decomposes the TBL-induced beam voltage into steady-state and transient components. Based on this model, we derive an optimization method to minimize power requirements, enabling the main-cavity TBL compensation to achieve performance levels comparable to those of broadband-cavity TBL compensation. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through two case studies: for an steady-state microbunching storage ring with a 7.5-MHz hardware half-bandwidth, the required single-cavity peak power is maintained at 158 kW, with normalized average radiation power improved from 78% to 97%; for the KEK light source storage ring with a 6-MHz bandwidth, the single-cavity peak power is optimized to 148 kW, successfully restoring the average bunch length from 31.1 to 40.9 ps. The proposed scheme establishes a highly efficient and cost-effective paradigm for TBL suppression, providing a promising technical pathway for next-generation light sources.

title: Space charge modeling method in 2.5D for scaling fixed-field alternating-gradient accelerators
abstract: Scaling fixed-field alternating-gradient accelerators (scaling FFAs) are promising candidates for high-intensity proton drivers, for which space charge effects are a key limitation of beam performance. For long bunches in circular accelerators, 2.5D space charge methods provide an efficient alternative to full 3D PIC methods by exploiting the large longitudinal-to-transverse aspect ratio of the bunch. In scaling FFAs, however, the reference closed orbit varies with particle energy, and the transverse and longitudinal directions are not directly available in cylindrical coordinates. Therefore, the longitudinal slicing and transverse planes required by a 2.5D model must be reconstructed dynamically, rather than defined from a single fixed reference orbit, which poses a central challenge for efficient 2.5D modeling in high-intensity scaling FFAs. This paper presents a new 2.5D space charge modeling method for high-intensity scaling FFAs and its implementation in the PyFFA code. The central idea is to replace the fixed reference orbit used in conventional 2.5D models with a dynamically reconstructed local reference frame based on a precomputed family of energy-dependent closed orbits. During tracking, this frame is updated according to the instantaneous particle state, enabling transverse Poisson equations to be solved consistently in this dynamic local coordinate system. The resulting space charge field is then transformed back to global cylindrical coordinates and applied in the tracking equations. Benchmarks of space charge fields, tune shifts, rms envelope evolution, and longitudinal phase-space evolution show good agreement with analytical results, validating the field calculation and its coupling to beam dynamics for long, arc-shaped bunches in scaling FFAs. The implemented model enables efficient studies of space charge effects on beam dynamics in high-intensity scaling FFAs.

title: Design criteria for a beam-driven resonant passive transverse deflector for longitudinal beam diagnostics
abstract: Conventional radio-frequency (rf) transverse deflecting structures provide high-resolution longitudinal beam diagnostics, but require externally generated high-power rf, waveguide distribution, synchronization, and input coupling at the operating frequency. We propose design criteria for a beam-driven resonant passive transverse deflector that does not require an external rf source. A leading drive bunch excites long-range wakefields in an off-axis periodic copper structure and a delayed witness bunch experiences the transverse wake near a zero crossing. The concept is based on the large temporal slope available from high-frequency wake components. A structure designed for installation after the second bunch compressor in the three-bunch-compressor layout of the European XFEL is optimized to place the zero crossing of the drive-bunch-induced transverse wake potential approximately one rf-bucket spacing of the 1.3 GHz linac behind the drive bunch. The selected geometry produces a multimode transverse kick dominated by TM-like modes. We use time-domain wake simulations, frequency-domain decomposition, cell-number scaling, mechanical-tolerance scans, orbit-offset studies, and uniform thermal scaling to determine the operating point and its sensitivity. For this geometry, the zero crossing occurs at s 0 ≃ 230.6 mm , with a per-cell temporal slope of S cell = 1.186 mV / ( pC fs cell ) . For a compact 1 m structure operated with a 250 pC drive bunch and a 700 MeV witness beam, the estimated temporal resolution is about 33 fs .

title: Comparison of hybrid and standard reconstruction methods on IXPE astrophysical data
abstract: A hybrid reconstruction algorithm combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) with standard moment analysis to improve the reconstruction of photoelectron tracks in the gas pixel detectors (GPDs) on board the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE). The method has been validated on laboratory calibration data, but its performance on astrophysical sources with known polarimetric properties has not yet been systematically characterized. We present the first comparison of hybrid and standard reconstruction methods on IXPE data of astrophysical point sources, with the aim of quantifying the improvement in polarimetric sensitivity as a function of energy. We analyzed two IXPE observations selected to probe complementary regimes: Her X-1, a bright and highly polarized accreting X-ray pulsar used as a quantitative benchmark, and the transient neutron star low-mass X-ray binary XTE J1701-461 in its soft state, a bright source with no detectable polarization used to measure residual systematic effects. For each source, we compared the normalized Stokes parameters, the degree of polarization (PD) and angle (PA), and the detection significance derived from the level 2 event files produced by both pipelines. For Her X-1, the hybrid method yields a consistently higher detection significance at all energies, with a statistically significant improvement above ∼2.83 keV. The significance ratio, R = σ_ /σ_ , deviates from unity by up to 9.3σ in the 2.83-4.00 keV bin, rising to R = 1.18 ± 0.03 at 5.66-8.00 keV at 6.2σ. For XTE J1701-461, both methods yield polarization degrees consistent with zero and significance ratios consistent with unity. Through a Fourier analysis, we identify some modes (m = 3, m = 6, m = 12, and m = 15) with power excesses in the hybrid angle distributions at low energies, which are significant at $>7σ$ relative to the standard method, while at 5-8 keV all modes are consistent with the expected noise level for both methods: these modes are amplified by CNN but do not propagate to the Stokes parameters. hyb std The hybrid method provides a measurable and statistically significant improvement in the polarimetric sensitivity for bright point sources that is fully consistent with the predictions from laboratory calibrations and equivalent to a sim20% increase in effective area without the additional cost of observation time. The hexagonal-grid modes are a geometric artifact of the GPD pixel structure and have no effect on polarimetric results since the additional modes are orthogonal to the polarization modes. The improvement is robustly detected for the bright source examined here (σ_ std For the unpolarized source in our sample (σ_ std the central significance increase is consistent with the same trend, but is not individually resolved at the available statistics. These findings confirm the readiness of the hybrid method for systematic application to IXPE astrophysical data.

title: Probing the G (3900) state in heavy-ion collisions
Multi-Threshold Sampling: Signal Space, Sampling Operators, and First Recorded Crossing-Time Distributions
abstract: Multi-threshold (MT) sampling records crossing times for parameter estimation and waveform reconstruction. We develop signal and observation spaces and stochastic crossing, timing, and selection operators with associated Markov kernels. Finite point measures accommodate variable crossing counts and preserve multiplicity after quantization. For nonhomogeneous Poisson photon arrivals with shared threshold noise, shared timing jitter before quantization, and identity selection, we derive exact first recorded crossing-time distributions. A Poisson series covers general admissible paths with a time-uniform truncation bound. For continuous paths, interval extrema give the exact cumulative distribution function (CDF) and a Fourier representation with contact corrections. A biexponential arrival-intensity and response model admits a two-dimensional first-crossing integral equation on arbitrary finite observation windows, with a unique bounded measurable solution and a Poisson-tail approximation bound. For continuous causal responses with finitely many analytic pieces and bounded first and second branch derivatives, we prove a conditional standard-deviation (SD) limit at first mean crossings with positive slope under relative threshold-noise and fine timing scales. For the biexponential model, its coefficient increases strictly on a parameter-uniform interval and, under a shape condition, up to the first mean peak. Scintillation experiments compare the calculated CDF and conditional SDs with independent waveform simulations on a window extending beyond the single-photon response peak.

title: Heavy quark collisional energy loss in a nonextensive quark-gluon plasma
abstract: Abstract In this study, we derive the longitudinal and transverse gluon self-energies and the corresponding dielectric functions for a nonextensive QGP, based on nonextensive statistical mechanics and a kinetic theory framework. The nonextensive parameter $q$ enters these quantities primarily through the modification of the Debye mass. Utilizing the derived dielectric functions, we then calculate the collisional energy loss for a heavy quark using two established formalisms: the plasma physics-based Thoma-Gyulassy formula and the thermal field theory-originated Kirzhnits-Thoma formula.Our results show that for both formalisms, the collisional energy loss increases with the nonextensive parameter$q$ with this enhancement being more significant at higher incident quark momenta and suppressed for a heavier quark mass. The energy loss predicted from the Kirzhnits-Thoma formula is substantially larger than that from the Thoma-Gyulassy formula, and the nonextensive effect on the energy loss is more pronounced in the former. Furthermore, the mass suppression of the nonextensive effect on the energy loss is weaker in the Kirzhnits-Thoma approach. These calculations demonstrate that nonextensive statistics can significantly alter the energy loss in the QGP. title: $\bar{D}$-meson Nucleon Scattering from Lattice QCD at the Physical Point
abstract: We report the first lattice QCD study of the $s$-wave scattering of the $\bar{D}$-meson and the nucleon at the physical point, utilizing (2+1)-flavor configurations generated by the HAL QCD collaboration with a pion mass of $m_\pi\simeq 137$ MeV and a lattice spacing of $a\simeq0.084$ fm. By applying the HAL QCD method to the four-point correlation function of the $\bar{D}N$ system, we obtain a leading-order potential of the derivative expansion of the interaction kernel, which is then used to extract the $s$-wave phase shifts of low-energy $\bar{D}N$ scattering. Both the isospin $I=0$ and $I=1$ channels have a short-range repulsive core and a shallow attractive pocket in the intermediate to long-range region, though the $I=0$ channel is more attractive than the $I=1$ channel. We also observe that the $\bar{D}N$ potential exhibits more attraction than the $KN$ potential, which is its analog in the strange sector. In terms of the $s$-wave phase shifts, the $I=0$ channel shows a weak attractive behavior in the low-energy region with a positive scattering length of $0.425 \pm 0.163 (_{-0.105}^{+0.129})$ fm, whereas the $I=1$ channel shows repulsion with a negative scattering length of $-0.235 \pm 0.046 (_{-0.007}^{+0.040})$ fm. No bound states are found in both isospin channels, indicating the absence of a pentaquark state in the $s$-wave $\bar{D}N$ system.

title: Non-Abelian Dirac oscillator in a uniform Yang–Mills background: exact spectrum and spin–isospin mixing
abstract: Abstract We study a planar Dirac oscillator in a uniform gauge background with an Abelian magnetic component and two non-Abelian amplitudes. The noncommuting spatial potentials generate a chromomagnetic curvature along T3 = τ3/2, while the temporal potential generates chromoelectric components proportional to their product. We derive the second-order stationary identity without discarding the isospin–orbit, diamagnetic, or scalar-potential terms. The first-order Hamiltonian, with minimal coupling, a Pauli interaction, or both, admits a conserved oscillator–spin–isospin operator and reduces to finite blocks. We obtain the exact secular equations, the exceptional lowest signed levels, and the leading avoided-crossing gaps. Minimal coupling produces transverse mixing already when the scalar amplitude vanishes; a gap proportional to the product of the amplitudes instead occurs at resonance in the pure Pauli model. We also solve a separately defined field-strength comparison operator. Its spin-dependent backbone does not commute with the transverse internal coupling, so its spectrum is not obtained by adding the isolated internal eigenvalues to the backbone energies. The mixed branches have quadratic weak-coupling shifts away from degeneracy. We distinguish gauge invariants from internal-basis labels and give conditional, spectrally resolved parameter examples, without claiming demonstrated graphene or atomic realizations.
source: Progress of Theoretical and Experimental Physics

title: Ballistic mixing: Stellar mergers drive internal mixing in extremely massive stars with implications for proto-globular cluster pollution
abstract: Extremely massive stars, with masses of 10 3 –10 4 M ⊙ , have been proposed as potential sources of the chemical enrichment associated with multiple populations in globular clusters. Early in the main sequence, these stars reach central temperatures of 65–75 MK, enabling nucleosynthesis through the CNO, NeNa, and MgAl cycles and producing abundance patterns similar to those observed in the so-called cluster’s second population. Among the leading formation channels for extremely massive stars are stellar mergers. We followed the formation of a ∼6700 M ⊙ star via 253 stellar mergers drawn from a direct N -body star cluster simulation with properties similar to the densest star clusters observed at redshift z ∼ 10. We evolved each star as a 1D stellar model and constructed the merger products from mixing and shock-heating prescriptions calibrated to 3D simulations of parabolic collisions. We find that entropy-based mixing efficiently transports nuclear-processed material from the convective core to the envelope, while merger-driven heating promotes chemical homogenization. As a result, the stellar surface becomes enriched with H-burning products, producing abundance patterns consistent with those observed in multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and supporting the role of extremely massive stars formed through mergers as potential sources of early chemical enrichment in proto-globular cluster-like conditions.

title: Proton generalized parton distributions from electromagnetic form factors: A theoretically constrained phenomenological reconstruction
abstract: We present a theoretically constrained phenomenological reconstruction of the unpolarized, chiral-even, leading-twist proton generalized parton distributions $H^q$ and $E^q$. At zero skewness, valence-quark distributions are combined with flavor-dependent exponential profiles calibrated simultaneously against phenomenological representations of the proton and neutron electromagnetic form factors. The construction imposes exact valence and anomalous-magnetic-moment normalizations, the low-scale condition $B^{u+d}(0)=0$, the required endpoint behavior, and the complete Gaussian impact-parameter positivity bound. The resulting parametrization provides a reasonable description of the electromagnetic form factors and their slopes while revealing the tension between strict GPD consistency and a precision reproduction of all low-$Q^2$ observables within the adopted ansatz. We extend the distributions to nonzero skewness using normalized double distributions and introduce an independent $D$-term to complete the relevant Mellin polynomials. We examine electromagnetic and energy--momentum-tensor form factors, impact-parameter distributions, positivity, polynomiality, and illustrative mechanical properties. The analysis distinguishes information constrained by electromagnetic data from additional assumptions governing skewness and the mechanical sector, thereby providing a transparent elastic baseline for future studies of nucleon-to-resonance transition GPDs.

title: Study of parametrized plasma response and regime for consistent stopping power models of α particles in ( D - T ) and p – 11 B fusion scenarios
abstract: Abstract This work develops a systematic parameterization of plasma response regimes in deuterium–tritium ( D - T ) and proton–boron ( p – 11 B) fusion plasmas using a set of dimensionless plasma parameters. These parameters describe the thermodynamic state of the plasma and its collective response properties, as well as the kinetic properties of energetic fusion-born alpha particles in terms of dimensionless ratios of characteristic velocities, collision/oscillation frequencies, and relevant interaction length scales. Special emphasis is put on α -electron and α -ion interaction metrics, which define the main energy-loss channels. By determining these dimensionless parameters across representative fusion-relevant density-temperature domains, the numerical analysis identifies the plasma regime controlling alpha-particle transport in ( D - T ) and p – 11 B plasmas. The results show that, under typical conditions for inertial confinement fusion, the plasmas are weakly to moderately coupled, weakly perturbed, and in a weakly non-degenerate regime, implying a consistent physical description where the energy exchange is governed by the collective response of the plasma. This study allows the identification of the operational domains in which reduced-stopping-power descriptions, such as the binary collision or dielectric response approaches, remain physically justifiable and numerically stable. This allows for the development of a physics-based framework in which to validate reduced transport models without the need for kinetic or quantum-level complexities. The parameterization aims at facilitating the integration of validated stopping models into advanced particle simulation toolboxes that include Monte Carlo approaches, such as GEANT4, for more valid virtual experiments in the study of fusion plasmas.

title: High-transformer-ratio plasma-based afterburner for extending X-ray free-electron laser photon energies to $\gtrsim$50 keV
abstract: Bright coherent X-rays in the $\gtrsim$50 keV range are highly desirable for applications in materials science, high-energy-density physics, and nuclear physics, but are difficult to obtain from present X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) facilities. Plasma-based afterburners offer a compact route to increasing the electron-beam energy, yet high transformer ratio (TR) operation is vulnerable to hosing instability, which can severely degrade the witness beam quality. We propose using a transversely elliptical driver beam to excite an elliptical nonlinear plasma wake with an axially varying focusing gradient, thereby suppressing the witness beam hosing through betatron decoherence. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations show that, for a 3 kA driver and a 2.35 kA witness beam with an rms length of 4 $\mathrm{\mu}$m and a beam separation of 94 $\mathrm{\mu}$m (TR $\approx 3$), this scheme can accelerate an 8 GeV witness beam to $\sim30$ GeV while nearly half of the electrons meet the XFEL requirements. Start-to-end simulations show that the resulting beam can drive $\gtrsim50$ keV XFEL radiation with peak powers of $\sim10$ GW and durations of $\sim10$ fs, even when quantum diffusion is included, offering a compact route to extend existing XFEL facilities to higher photon energies.

title: Estimation of Very High Energy Electron (VHEE) beam parameters using an in-air screen
abstract: Very high energy electron (VHEE) beams offer several promising properties for radiotherapy. Accurate beam delivery requires a beam model that accounts for scattering along the beam propagation path. This work develops and validates a beam model incorporating Multiple Coulomb Scattering (MCS) to estimate beam parameters. MCS is incorporated as an additive term to the covariance matrix transformation for a drift space, allowing conventional quadrupole scans to estimate beam parameters in the presence of a downstream scatterer. The scattering correction factor is fitted to Monte Carlo (MC) simulations for a range of materials and thicknesses. The model is then validated by recovering the initial beam parameters from simulated quadrupole scans of a realistic beamline. Finally, the method is applied to in-air screen measurements at the Pulsed Energetic Electrons for Research (PEER) end station of the Australian Synchrotron. After fitting the correction factors, the mean and standard deviation of the estimation errors for the final emittance, diameter, divergence, and mean kinetic energy were $(-0.06 \pm 3.17)\%$, $(0.15 \pm 0.66)\%$, $(0.18 \pm 2.18)\%$, and $(-0.03 \pm 0.06)\%$, respectively. Simulated quadrupole scans successfully recovered the initial beam parameters, with errors of at most $13\%$. PEER measurements yielded emittance estimates ranging from $0.238$ to $1.753~\mathrm{mm\,mrad}$ across scans, which were within the expected range. Following an initial quadrupole scan, the method allows the in-air beam size to be estimated for other quadrupole configurations. Further work is required to improve the consistency and reliability of the experimental estimates.

title: Unsupervised Neural Operators for Rotating Relativistic Stars: High-Fidelity Equation of State Inference and Pulsar Spin Evolution at Scale
abstract: Observed populations of rotating neutron stars~(NSs) with millisecond-order periods are powerful probes of fundamental physics. Mass-radius measurements inform poorly constrained properties of degenerate nuclear matter, whereas high-fidelity population synthesis connects unknowns in NS formation and binary evolution to large radio-timing surveys. However, repeated structure calculations are prohibitive due to the computational cost of solving the highly coupled partial differential equations of axisymmetric general relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium that govern rotating NS interiors. Non-rotating calculations or approximate rotational corrections can bias equation of state inference and limit the fidelity of population synthesis in tracing the evolutionary history of progenitors and propagating equation of state uncertainties. In this \textit{Letter}, we develop physics-informed neural operators that can solve the axisymmetric problem with high accuracy and negligible computational cost. \textit{Our solvers are trained in a fully unsupervised setting, with the training objective informed solely by the partial differential equations, and achieve a $10^3\times$ speed-up with negligible accuracy loss}. These solvers enable scalable EoS inference that self-consistently accounts for rotation and repeated stellar-structure calculations during binary evolution, making spin predictions that account for rotational structure and EoS uncertainties computationally accessible to population synthesis.

title: Search for $\mathrm{GeV}$-scale axion-like particles in PbPb collisions
abstract: A search is performed for the production of axion-like particles with masses in the range 3-10 GeV using PbPb collision data recorded by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $0.228~\mathrm{nb}^{-1}$ and a nucleon-nucleon centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02$ TeV. This is the first search for axion-like particles produced exclusively by two photons ($\gamma\gamma\to a\to\gamma\gamma$) in the forward direction. It extends sensitivity to previously unexplored regions of the parameter space, probing axion-like particle masses and couplings down to 3.0 GeV and $3.2\times10^{-4}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$, respectively. This result provides the most stringent limits to date on the production of axion-like particles from exclusive photon-photon fusion processes with masses between 3 and 5 GeV.

title: Report of the National Lab Accelerator Study Group for a Muon Collider
abstract: The National Laboratory Accelerator Study Group (NLASG) was established to assess the accelerator research and development required to advance a future high-energy Muon Collider, with particular emphasis on opportunities for coordinated contributions from U.S. national laboratories. This report examines the principal accelerator subsystems, their technical maturity, and the critical challenges that must be addressed before proceeding to a technical design. Topics include the proton driver, target and capture system, muon cooling, acceleration, collider ring, and machine-detector interface. The study identifies priority R&D activities, evaluates opportunities to leverage existing laboratory capabilities and accelerator infrastructure, and outlines a staged approach to technology demonstrations and integrated system validation. Particular emphasis is placed on developing a coordinated national research strategy that complements international efforts and establishes a technically credible path toward a future Muon Collider.

title: Reduced Order Hysteretic Magnetization Model for Composite Superconductors
abstract: In this paper, we propose the Reduced Order Hysteretic Magnetization (ROHM) model to describe the magnetization and instantaneous power loss of composite superconductors subject to time-varying magnetic fields. Once the parameters of the ROHM model are fixed based on reference simulations, it allows to directly compute the macroscopic response of composite superconductors without the need to solve the detailed current density distribution. It can then be used as part of a homogenization method in large-scale superconducting models to significantly reduce the computational effort compared to detailed simulations. In this contribution, we focus on the case of a strand with twisted superconducting filaments subject to a time-varying transverse magnetic field. We propose two variations of the ROHM model: (i) a rate-independent model that reproduces hysteresis in the filaments, and (ii) a rate-dependent model that generalizes the first level by also reproducing dynamic effects due to coupling and eddy currents. We then describe the implementation and inclusion of the ROHM model in a finite element framework, discuss how to deduce the model parameters, and finally demonstrate the capabilities of the approach in terms of accuracy and efficiency over a wide range of excitation frequencies and amplitudes.

title: Impedance of multilayer cylindrical structures with a material-filled beam region
abstract: Beam-coupling impedances in material media are relevant for ionization-cooling channels of a future muon collider, where the beam propagates in matter rather than vacuum. We extend the cylindrical field-matching formalism for multilayer structures to the case of a material-filled beam region surrounded by external layers with arbitrary electromagnetic properties. Relative to the vacuum formulation, the usual factor $1/\gamma^2$ is replaced by the material-dependent factor $F=1/\varepsilon_1-\mu_1\beta^2$, and the radial propagation constant is modified accordingly. Analytical expressions are obtained for the monopolar longitudinal and dipolar transverse impedances, with the surrounding structure encoded through reflection coefficients determined by field matching. The formalism reduces to the known vacuum and perfectly conducting limits in the appropriate cases. Representative calculations are presented for absorber-relevant configurations, illustrating the dependence on the material properties of both the beam region and the surrounding layers. In particular, a finite beam-region conductivity can generate a real impedance component and reverse the sign of the imaginary space-charge impedance, while sufficiently high permittivity can give rise to resonant structures associated with oscillatory radial fields. The effect of finite-conductivity surroundings is also examined, showing the approach towards the perfectly conducting limit as the external conductivity is increased. The applicability of the infinite-length approximation is also discussed by comparison with finite-length mode-matching results.

title: Characterizing Gravitational Wave Electromagnetic Counterparts with the Schmidt Observatory System
abstract: The emergence of gravitational wave (GW) multimessenger astronomy, marked by the detection of GW170817 and its associated kilonova, has opened a new window into the physics of compact binary mergers. Building a statistical population of kilonovae remains a challenge, limited by the low neutron star merger detection rates and the rapid evolution of these faint transients. The former problem will be overcome with upcoming LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA (LVK) sensitivity improvements leading to the fifth Observing Run (O5), while the latter will be addressed by the Schmidt Observatory System (including the Argus Array, the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA), and the Lazuli Space Observatory), in addition to ongoing and upcoming surveys (including the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time). Using simulations of expected kilonovae at LVK O5 sensitivity, we find that Argus and Rubin could detect binary neutron star kilonovae at a rate of 0.3-4.2 yr$^{-1}$ and 0.6-7.0 yr$^{-1}$ respectively. For neutron star-black hole mergers, Rubin could detect up to 1 kilonova per year. Lazuli will be able to characterize this kilonova population down to $g \sim 26$ mag as early as 12 hours post merger. Additionally, $\sim35\%$ of these events are expected to exhibit a jet afterglow that will be detectable by DSA. We further characterize kilonova spectra to determine observable features of heavy element production. Finally, we develop an observing strategy that combines high cadence imaging and spectral monitoring, maximizing Lazuli's ability to constrain ejecta properties and composition of GW counterparts with reasonable observing time.

title: Brilliance for adaptive computational research in accelerator physics
abstract: Computational research requires repeated decisions about models, calculations and the interpretation of results. We introduce Brilliance, an agent that combines large language models, reusable physics expertise and numerical simulation to construct and revise investigations in accelerator physics. Starting from a detailed expert-specified request, Brilliance develops an ideal storage-ring lattice meeting the specified emittance ceiling and sampled nonlinear-acceptance criteria after revising optics that fail particle-tracking tests. Further scientist-guided exploration produces a candidate with a natural emittance of 6.51 pm rad and millimeter-scale transverse acceptance, while exposing unresolved momentum-acceptance limitations. Using measured responses from the High Energy Photon Source, Brilliance also performs offline optics calibration consistent with an independent specialist analysis. An expert-module ablation examines how reusable domain knowledge influences research choices and outcomes. Here, we demonstrate a practical route to scientist-agent collaboration in sustained numerical research.

title: Beam Transport Through a Quadrupole with Offsets in Both Transverse Planes
abstract: In accelerator switchyards with shared magnets, a beam may traverse a quadrupole with offsets in both transverse planes, a configuration that cannot be represented by a single conventional horizontal or vertical combined-function bend. Such an off-axis quadrupole bends the reference trajectory and generates dispersion simultaneously in both planes. We derive a compact analytical $6\times6$ transfer matrix about the curved reference trajectory. The model is formulated in Bishop coordinates using a weak-curvature approximation that retains the longitudinal variation of both reference-curvature components and the resulting dispersion in both transverse planes. The analytical linear model is compared with a sliced representation based on conventional second-order combined-function bend maps and with direct numerical integration of the Lorentz equations in the ideal Cartesian quadrupole field.

title: Operational Challenges in Efficient and Sustainable Operation of the Event Processing Nodes GPU Farm at the ALICE Experiment
abstract: ALICE's Event Processing Nodes (EPN) farm is CERN's largest GPU computing facility by capacity, comprising 350 GPU-based nodes and 2800 GPUs delivering approximately a total of 48\,PFLOP/s. It has successfully enabled real-time processing of heavy-ion collisions at 50\,kHz during LHC Run~3. The facility was designed for sustainability, extended hardware lifetime, and reduced operational overhead. High availability is supported by a robust technical architecture and well-defined operational practices, ensuring reliable and continuous operation throughout data taking.

title: The kinematic Kelvin-Helmholtz instability-driven dynamo: implications for merging compact objects
abstract: Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers excite a Kelvin--Helmholtz instability (KHI) in the shear layer between them. It is parasitized upon by the magnetic field to form a powerful magnetic dynamo. Using a large ensemble of high-resolution visco-resistive KHI-driven dynamo simulations we construct analytical, asymptotic in Reynolds number ($\rm{Re}$) models for the magnetic field growth rates and mean vertical field dynamo onset times. Our models suggest that in the $\rm{Re} \gg 1$ limit, the mean vertical field is seeded immediately, kinematic growth rates become asymptotic in $\rm{Re}$, and the dynamo moves out of the kinematic stage on $\mathcal{O}(0.1\,\rm{ms})$ timescales, readily attaining magnetar-strength fields during this transition. This suggests that most global BNS merger simulations are not time-resolving the correct KHI-driven dynamo regime.

title: The Space-Based Time-Domain Revolution in Astrophysics
abstract: Space-based time-domain telescopes such as CoRoT, Kepler/K2 and TESS have profoundly impacted astrophysics over the past two decades. Continuous light curves with high cadence and high photometric precision are now available for millions of sources within our galaxy and beyond. In addition to revolutionizing exoplanet science, the data have enabled breakthroughs ranging from the solar system to stellar interiors, the transient universe, and active galaxies. The key summary points of this review are: (1) Stellar astrophysics has been transformed by the ability to probe the internal structures of stars, test the physics of stellar convection, connect stellar rotation and magnetic activity, and reveal complex variability in young stars. (2) Ages of stellar populations probe the formation history of our Milky Way, and binary star variability enables the detection of "dark" galactic populations such as stellar-mass black holes and neutron stars. (3) Early-time observations of explosive transients provide new insights into the progenitors of supernovae, while the quasi-periodic variability of galaxies probes the physics of accretion processes onto supermassive black holes and the tidal disruption of stars. (4) Observations of solar system objects reveal asteroid compositions through their rotation periods and amplitudes, constrain the cloud structure of ice giants, and allow the discovery of new objects in the outer solar system. (5) Open data policies and software have contributed to remarkable scientific productivity and enabled discoveries by citizen scientists, including new exoplanets and exotic variability in mature Sun-like stars.

title: Searching for Signatures of i-process Nucleosynthesis in Metal-Rich, Lead-rich Barium Stars
abstract: The intermediate neutron-capture process ($i$-process) has been invoked to explain the peculiar compositions of carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars enriched in both slow- ($s$) and rapid- ($r$) neutron-capture elements. Recent literature has questioned its operation at higher metallicities, but observational evidence remains limited. We analyse Gemini/GHOST and McDonald/Tull spectra of six $\rm -0.7 < [Fe/H] < -0.1$ stars identified in GALAH by their extreme Ba and Eu (or Sm) compositions ($\gtrsim$10$\times$ solar). We also reanalyse archival spectra of two literature $i$-process candidates. We determine abundances in up to 42 elements (Li through Pb), $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, and Mg isotopic ratios, and compare to literature barium and CEMP stars and multiple asymptotic giant branch (AGB) model grids. Three stars exhibit extreme [Pb/Fe] (+1.79$\pm$0.19 to +2.50$\pm$0.32 dex), and two extreme [Eu/Fe] (+1.10$\pm$0.11 to +1.30$\pm$0.11 dex), distinguishing them from typical metal-rich barium stars. Two of these three exhibit abundance patterns that are inconsistent with $s$-process models and best explained by existing $i$-process predictions. The remaining sample is either consistent with $s$-process enrichment or suggestive of atomic diffusion. Both literature candidates are well-fit by the $i$-process model, but conventional $s$-process enrichment cannot be excluded. Our findings reinforce that metal-rich AGB stars contribute to the production of elements classically attributed to the $r$-process. These results identify promising candidates for $i$-process enrichment near solar metallicity and motivate additional $i$-process models to understand the contribution of this nucleosynthetic process to the chemical evolution of the Milky Way disk.

title: Reduced vortex descriptors linking polycrystallinity in magnetic nanoparticles with polarized magnetic small-angle neutron scattering
abstract: Analytical vortex models reduce polarized magnetic small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) from nanoparticle ensembles to a small set of texture descriptors. In this work, we apply this reduction to micromagnetic simulations of polycrystalline iron oxide nanoflowers at a fixed particle size and examine how a controlled parametrization of multigrain disorder is reflected in the remanent descriptors. The particles are represented by explicit Voronoi microstructures, and intraparticle disorder is varied through the intergrain exchange coupling and anisotropy-axis coherence. Fitting each remanent magnetization state to a hyperbolic vortex model reveals a predominantly two-channel organization: The intergrain exchange coupling is associated mainly with the radial vortex profile, whereas the anisotropy-axis coherence is associated mainly with the orientational moment of the vortex-axis distribution. The normalized spin-flip SANS cross sections are accurately represented by independent fits of the analytical linear-vortex SANS expression obtained from the first-order expansion of the hyperbolic profile. The fitted orientational descriptor agrees closely with its independent real-space estimate, whereas the corresponding radial descriptors exhibit a strong global nonlinear relation. This separation identifies which information from the micromagnetic vortex textures is robustly retained by the reduced analytical representation.

title: Neutron star cooling with medium-modified Urca rates
abstract: We study the effects of in-medium modification of the elementary cooling processes on observable properties of isolated neutron stars. We deduce the neutron star mass distributions compatible with the cooling analysis and compare with current theoretical models. We conclude that current cooling data require fast direct Urca cooling, moderated by proton superfluidity, to be active in most neutron stars, and that the DU onset threshold must lie below canonical masses. In that case medium modifications of modified Urca rates are practically insignificant, but the nn Bremsstrahlung rate plays a dominant role.

title: Development of a ray-based linear gain post-processor to model stimulated Raman scattering in multiple emission directions
abstract: Stimulated Raman sidescattering has become a major concern in ignition-scale inertial confinement fusion (ICF) experiments due to its detrimental role in generating suprathermal electrons, which can preheat the fuel capsule and degrade implosion performance. This paper introduces RAMUD (RAman in MUltiple Directions), a numerically efficient, ray-based, linear gain post-processor, which models stimulated Raman scattering using a ray tracing approach, enabling the study of Raman light emitted in both backscattering and sidescattering geometries in a 2D spatial domain. The code comprises two core modules: the first one calculates the refraction of the laser and Raman light, using the standard eikonal ray tracing equation based on user-defined intial scattering angles and plasma parameters typically obtained from radiation-hydrodynamic simulations. The second module employs a path integral method to compute linear convective gains, quantifying the amplification of the scattered light. By processing the outputs of these calculations (Raman wavelength, final propagation angle after refraction, gain values, transmitted power after inverse Bremsstrahlung absorption), RAMUD generates numerical Raman gain spectra that can be directly compared to experimental measurements from ICF experiments. We describe RAMUD's operational principle and test its accuracy against theoretical predictions in a few test cases. We next apply the code to model SRS in a planar direct drive experiment performed at the National Ignition Facility, where intense sidescattering has been reportedly observed. The spectra computed using RAMUD show good agreement with the measured spectra and align closely with the experimental interpretations.

title: Emergent Transfer of a Physics Foundation Model from Simulation to Laboratory Turbulence
abstract: Whether physics foundation models can be usefully deployed on laboratory experiments remains an open question for scientific machine learning (ML). We test this question on the Rayleigh-Taylor instability (RTI), a ubiquitous and demanding fluid instability seen from tabletop flows to supernova explosions, in which small perturbations at a density interface grow into chaotic, multiscale mixing as a lighter fluid accelerates into a heavier one. Standard ML models struggle with RTI, and despite over a century of theoretical, numerical, and experimental work, it carries an unresolved discrepancy between simulation and experiment: the late-time mixing growth rate, $\alpha$, measured in most laboratory experiments ($\sim$ 0.06-0.07), is roughly three times the value from idealized direct numerical simulations (DNS, $\sim$ 0.02). The gap's origin remains debated. These properties make RTI a stringent test for a question that matters well beyond RTI: can foundation models trained only on simulations generalise to sparse, messy, and noisy laboratory settings? We finetune Walrus, a foundation model for continuum dynamics, on three or fewer DNS realizations and recover key RTI physics over long rollouts. Applied zero-shot to sliding-barrier laboratory data, the finetuned model leaves the DNS-like regime and enters the observed growth band, having never seen a single experimental sample. These results provide independent, data-driven evidence that initial conditions play a crucial role in the longstanding sim-experiment gap in $\alpha$. The model also generalises zero-shot to stable stratification, a buoyancy regime absent from training, correctly slowing mixing-layer growth. Together, our results show that foundation models can generalise well beyond their training data, predicting laboratory behavior and unseen physical regimes, opening new ways to probe longstanding simulation-experiment gaps.

title: What Does Precision Spectroscopy Actually Constrain about X17 Couplings?
abstract: Can precision spectroscopy disentangle the individual couplings of the X17 boson? Within a leading one-body model, we combine electronic and muonic spectroscopy of hydrogen, deuterium and helium with lepton magnetic moments. We show that hydrogen-deuterium comparisons can lose neutron sensitivity through cancellations, while the combined observables restore generic local identifiability without guaranteeing finite individual bounds. The unrestricted fit admits formally unbounded nucleon-coupling directions, some of which violate the assumptions underlying the physical model. Finite-coupling tests nevertheless reveal statistically compatible solutions, with bounds dependent on nuclear responses and physical assumptions. Our results establish what precision measurements genuinely constrain and what additional information is required to extract meaningful limits on X17 couplings.

title: Photon-nucleon entanglement in Compton scattering at low and high energies
abstract: We study spin-spin entanglement in the final state photon-nucleon system in Compton scattering, both at low energy below the pion threshold and at high energy in perturbative QCD to next-to-leading order. We first establish a no-go theorem showing that, for any spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ target, entanglement cannot be generated in unpolarized Compton scattering if the scattering amplitudes are real. We then consider polarized Compton scattering off the electron, the proton and the neutron. At low energy, we uncover a rich variety of maximally entangled Bell states and their unitary equivalents realized across different regions of the kinematic plane. Interestingly, the proton and neutron targets exhibit distinct patterns of entanglement. In the neutron case, the electric and magnetic polarizabilities dramatically influence the pattern and even the existence of entanglement. This suggests that entanglement can serve as a novel tool for investigating the detailed electromagnetic properties of the nucleons.
