title: SpikePID: Real-Time Neuromorphic Cluster Counting in Future Drift Chambers
abstract: Cluster counting ($dN/dx$) measures discrete ionization occurrences along a charged particle track traversing a gaseous medium and is currently being proposed to serve particle identification (PID) in next-generation drift chambers, as it is expected to offer higher separation power than the traditional approach based on the ionization energy loss measurement ($dE/dx$), which has intrinsically larger statistical fluctuations. However, measuring $dN/dx$ in drift chambers proposed for future colliders requires high-resolution waveforms, which result in very large data rates. Running the reconstruction at the edge would drastically reduce the bandwidth required to transmit data off the detector. In this paper, we introduce SpikePID, a neuromorphic computing approach applying spiking neural networks (SNNs) to this task due to their inherently sparse computing and processing nature. We show that an SNN with only 529 parameters improves the kaon-pion separation power by 17% over the traditional derivative-based method and by 4% over an MLP that has $8.6\times$ more parameters. When synthesized to an FPGA, it uses an order of magnitude fewer resources than the MLP, and has an inference latency compatible with the constraints of future collider experiments, making the SNN an excellent algorithmic candidate for real-time data readout in future drift chambers.

title: Sealed, Lightweight gRPC-Based Muon Telescopes for Muography Applications
abstract: Portable muon detection systems are increasingly in demand for muography applications in environments requiring flexible installation and transportability. We present the ongoing development and implementation of portable muon tracking systems based on glass Resistive Plate Chambers (gRPCs). The work addresses the fabrication and assembly of compact, position-sensitive RPC detectors, along with their performance when operated with a standard gas mixture and coupled to external front-end electronics and a scalable multi-channel data-acquisition system. The system design prioritizes modular construction, mechanical robustness, operational safety, autonomous functionality, and cost-effectiveness. Measurements with atmospheric muons demonstrated stable detector performance and reliable tracking capability, confirming the suitability of this architecture for muographic measurements. We conclude with an outlook on further developments of the detection system.

title: SCRAMJet: An Ultra Low Latency JetClass-Scale Transformer for the HL-LHC Level-1 Trigger
abstract: Level-1 Triggers at the LHC classify collisions within a few microseconds on FPGAs, where a network is a fully unrolled circuit whose cost is area rather than time. We present SCRAMJet, a transformer encoder that replaces multi-head attention with a low-rank projection, trains under per-parameter learned fixed-point quantization, and compiles to Verilog with distributed arithmetic optimization. On the ten-class JetClass dataset it reaches $71.4 \pm 0.6\%$ accuracy with 0.157M multiply-accumulates, 6.1 accuracy points above the strongest published resource-constrained model at an eighth of the operations, and meets timing on a Virtex UltraScale+ VU13P at 147 ns using 25.7% of the logic. We also show that resource-aware training silently removes attention channels: one whose learned bit-width reaches zero still carries signal during training but is absent from the compiled circuit, so the loss never sees it go. We call these virtual channels, and a floor on the attention datalane that prevents them is worth 3.1 accuracy points at matched budget. Code and trained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Aaddy-1/hgq-jetformer.

title: Optimal Fan-Out and Break-Even Routing Loss in Waveguide-Integrated Ge-on-Si SPAD Arrays
abstract: Splitting a waveguide mode over several Ge-on-Si single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) relieves dead-time saturation but multiplies dark counts. We quantify this trade-off with the asymptotic count-based information rate, which prices dark counts and dead time in one unit and is attained by an optimally weighted moment estimator. For a non-paralyzable pixel, the information per pre-dead-time signal event peaks at a signal rate $y^*=\sqrt{D(D+1/\tau)}$ with exact efficiency $(\sqrt{1+D\tau}-\sqrt{D\tau})^2$, which sets the optimal fan-out and a critical flux above which equal splitting is optimal. We then compare four routing architectures on 64 simulated 16-pixel arrays: an equal passive tree, static trees (uncalibrated, and an idealized calibration-informed benchmark), an ideal programmable tree, and a thermo-optic Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) tree with 1.32 dB excess loss. Ideal programmability gains up to 15.9 dB over equal splitting at low flux. At one known flux, however, the calibrated static splitter beats the MZI tree by 0.14-2.7 dB, and the penalty tends to twice the excess loss when dark counts dominate. In ensemble-median worst-case regret, the MZI tree breaks even only for flux windows wider than 2.55 decades, and not within six decades above about 3.4 dB excess loss. Event-level Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the count statistics and the predicted estimator variances within bootstrap confidence intervals. Sensitivity analyses cover dark-count level, heterogeneity, detector model and random seed. All results are simulations with representative literature parameters.

title: Muography Simulations for Carbon Capture and Storage Monitoring
abstract: Muography can monitor CO2 storage through reservoir density changes, but site-scale simulations are costly: reservoirs can be deep and borehole detectors are small. We address both with two approaches. First, a two-stage workflow splits the kilometer-scale simulation: a fast code transports muons through the overburden, and a general-purpose Monte Carlo code through the reservoir and detectors. Second, a geometric filter at the source keeps only muons whose direction and position let them reach the detectors, within a margin for multiple scattering, and a range cut removes those with too little energy. Both are available in the UCMuon simulation suite for muon generation, filtering and transport. At a deep (800-1000 m) and a shallow (65 m) CO2 storage site, each approach reduces the computing time about 700-fold, and the filtered simulation gives the same hit rate as a full one, as long as the margin exceeds the muons' sideways scattering drift.

title: Localized anomaly detection with a calorimeter normalizing flow
abstract: Normalizing flows trained as fast calorimeter simulators also give the likelihood of each shower, which can serve as an anomaly score. Because this likelihood sums over every voxel, a signal confined to a few voxels can be lost in the fluctuations of the rest of the shower. For example, in a public benchmark dataset in which a long-lived neutral particle decays to two photons, the CaloFlow likelihood used in previous work selects less than 5% of the signal at a background efficiency of $10^{-3}$ when the particle has the largest simulated mass and decays at or just behind the front face of the calorimeter. In this work, we define a regional anomaly score by summing the squared latent coordinates of the same flow within small detector regions around the point where the particle enters the calorimeter, with the threshold set using background showers alone. At the same background efficiency, this regional anomaly score selects more than 95% of the signal. The per-coordinate likelihood terms, summed over the same regions, perform equally well, but the squared latent coordinates have a known distribution for background showers and clearly illustrate when a shower departs from it. Therefore, normalizing flows may be sensitive to new physics, even if the global likelihood is not.

title: Highly polarized epithermal neutron beam using polarized 3He gas at J-PARC
abstract: We have realized a highly polarized epithermal neutron beam using an in-situ polarized 3He spin filter at the high-intensity pulsed neutron facility J-PARC. A neutron polarization exceeding 80% was achieved for epithermal neutrons with energies below 1 eV, including a polarization of 86.4 $\pm$ 0.5% for 0.75 eV neutrons, which corresponds to the resonance energy of the p-wave compound state in the 139La+n system. The spin filter consisted of a 20-cm-long, 3.2-atm 3He gas cell polarized on the beamline using a compact laser-optics system for spin-exchange optical pumping (SEOP). A 3He polarization of approximately 78% was stably maintained on the beamline for more than 100 hours. The polarized epithermal neutron beam developed in this work provides a powerful tool for studies of discrete symmetry violations, including measurements of enhanced parity violation in neutron absorption by medium-heavy nuclei such as 139La and searches for time-reversal symmetry violation in neutron-nucleus systems.

title: Feed-forward active magnetic shielding
abstract: Measurement of small magnetic fields requires shielding. For example, magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures small fields arising within the brain, in the presence of environmental fields several orders of magnitude larger. A common solution is passive shielding, but its cost, bulk and limited effectiveness motivate the alternative approach of active shielding, which comes in two flavours: feed-back and feed-forward. In feed-back shielding (the most common design), coils are driven from sensors that measure the corrected field. In feed-forward shielding (less common), coils are driven from sensors that measure the uncorrected field. The latter has the potential of providing better performance, but its implementation is hobbled by an inevitable coupling between coils and reference sensors. This paper describes an approach that employs a data-driven ``decoupling matrix" to suppress the coupling, enabling greater flexibility to achieve effective shielding across a wide frequency range. The method is evaluated by simulation, first using a simplified "flat world" in which the principle is clearly visualised, and then based on the more realistic geometry of a standard MEG system. Performance appears to be limited only by spatial sampling and numerical resolution. The method, which is data-driven and does not require geometric calculations, tight-tolerance fabrication, or manual calibration, is complementary with standard feed-back shielding methods. Active shielding is of particular interest in the context of a new generation of optically-pumped magnetometers (OPM), as the lower cost and reduced constraints of these new systems relative to SQUID-based systems provide an incentive to likewise reduce the cost and constraints of shielding.

title: Fabrication and characterization of a micro-boiling meter for heat transfer measurements on a single nucleation site
abstract: Accurate characterization of heat transfer during pool boiling requires sensors capable of resolving rapid transients and highly localized thermal events. Conventional approaches often suffer from limited spatial resolution and slow thermal response due to intermediate material layers. To overcome these limitations and obtain accurate measurements of surface temperature and heat flux during pool boiling studies, we used a boiling meter. Two of these consist of commercially available sensors. To improve the study of vapor bubble dynamics, a third boiling meter was designed, dimensioned, and microfabricated. It was fabricated on a Borofloat 33-silicon composite substrate featuring a suspended Borofloat membrane with a central 200 $\mu$m micropillar and a laser-ablated nucleation site (100 $\mu$m x 115 $\mu$m). Two platinum resistance temperature detectors (Pt-RTDs) were integrated on both sides of the substrate to enable direct, localized, and time-resolved measurements of wall temperature and heat flux during bubble formation. Characterization of the microfabricated boiling meter was carried out in controlled radiative environment and in pool boiling. The microfabricated device exhibited a thermal characteristic time of around 200 ms in radiative tests (more than 30 times shorter under similar operating conditions than the times found with boiling meters composed of commercial sensors), but was able to capture a bubble frequency of 26 Hz, which validates its ability to resolve transient thermal events. Its suspended glass-membrane structure, combined with the direct liquid-RTD interface, provides both high temporal resolution and spatial sensitivity, essential for capturing the short timescales of bubble nucleation, growth, and departure.

title: Dual-Band Mid-Infrared Imaging for Measurement of Fuel Concentration and Temperature in a Supersonic Cavity
abstract: A dual-band mid-infrared absorption imaging method is demonstrated for spatially resolved measurement of ethylene concentration and temperature in a Mach-2 cavity flow. The method used narrowband filters selected to exploit the differing in-band temperature sensitivities of ethylene absorption, together with a broadband infrared source and high-frame-rate mid-wave infrared camera. Temperature-dependent, filter-weighted absorption cross-sections were used to measure two-dimensional ethylene number density and temperature fields. Measurements were obtained for cavity, curtain, and discrete fuel-injection configurations, including cases with the leading edge of a quasi-steady shock near the cavity. Cavity equivalence ratio measurements agreed well with independent extractive measurements and reproduced trends previously observed using hyperspectral imaging. A complementary single-band implementation using a temperature-independent filter provided instantaneous ethylene concentration fields at 100 Hz and revealed intermittent reductions in cavity equivalence ratio associated with plume deflection by the shock train leading edge. The dual-band approach provides quantitative full-field measurements with substantially simpler spectral instrumentation than hyperspectral imaging while retaining flexibility for time-resolved flow measurements.

title: Cryogenic Optoelectronic Characterization of InGaAsP LEDs for Low-Energy Detector Calibration
abstract: We measured the emission spectra and current-voltage (IV) characteristics of commercial InGaAsP LEDs in a cryostat over a temperature range from 7 K to 300 K. At a constant operating current of 3.3 mA, the peak emission wavelength of the 1200 nm (1650 nm) LED decreased from 1202.3 +/- 0.5 nm (1665.5 +/- 0.6 nm) at 300 K to 1143.1 +/- 0.3 nm (1539.5 +/- 2.2 nm) at 7 K, demonstrating a strong temperature dependence. The cut-in voltage increased systematically with decreasing temperature, in agreement with conventional diode theory. To assess junction self-heating effects, we conducted pulsed IV measurements at different duty cycles. The extracted apparent series resistance showed a clear duty-cycle dependence, whereas the cut-in voltage remained unchanged within experimental uncertainty, indicating that self-heating primarily influenced the IV slope rather than the cut-in voltage. These results quantitatively characterize the thermal behavior of both the spectral peak and key electrical parameters, supporting the application of InGaAsP LEDs as cryogenic calibration light sources.

title: Characterization of Next Generation Power Over Fiber Systems under Cryogenic Conditions for Advanced Physics Instrumentation
abstract: The successful application of Power-over-Fiber (PoF) technology to power photon detection systems in DUNE prototypes operating under high-voltage and cryogenic conditions has laid the groundwork for the next generation of PoF systems operating in harsh environments. This paper presents the characterization of the main components of a new PoF system operating at 1470 and 1550 nm, including the measurement of the electrical-to-optical conversion efficiency of laser transmitters, the optical-to-electrical conversion efficiency of commercial optical power converters (OPCs), and the estimation of optical fiber attenuation under cryogenic conditions. In addition, a detailed characterization of the response of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) to light leakage from optical fibers and OPCs is presented, using 808 nm as a reference to evaluate the reduction in the SiPM response at longer wavelengths. The results of this work provide a foundation for the development of next-generation PoF systems capable of powering electronics and electrical systems for future high-energy physics experiments. In addition, the electrical isolation, low-noise operation, and long-term reliability of PoF technology could motivate its application in other research fields requiring remote power delivery under cryogenic conditions, as well as in systems where infrared photons could affect their performance.

title: A Scalable Two-Stage Back-End Architecture for 400GbE Data Acquisition Systems
abstract: A primary challenge in High Energy Physics (HEP) data acquisition is the aggregation of numerous low-speed (10 Gb/s) radiation-hard data links into high-speed back-end interfaces. While high-end FPGAs traditionally perform this task, transceiver density and speed in modern devices can limit cost-effective scaling. This study proposes a two-stage architecture that utilizes mid-range FPGAs for decoding and Ethernet conversion, followed by a Microchip META-DX2+ Ethernet PHY that aggregates these streams into a 400 GbE interface. This study evaluates the design's performance, validating it as a scalable and cost-effective architecture for next-generation HEP data acquisition systems.

title: Wavelength dependent characterization of alkali antimonide photocathodes in an S-band rf gun
Torque lags from magnetic unlocking in neutron stars and gravitational-wave smearing
abstract: In canonical twisted-torus models of hydromagnetic equilibrium in neutron stars, the toroidal field is confined to regions where the poloidal field lines are closed. As spindown torques applied at the stellar surface need not be communicated efficiently to such magnetically unlocked regions, toroidal zones or magnetic voids can rotate faster than the electromagnetically braked part of the star. Continuous gravitational radiation from the associated non-corotating quadrupole can therefore be emitted at higher frequencies than poloidal ones to a degree that depends on the diffusive microphysics controlling angular momentum transport. Dissipative processes can suppress long-lived lags, and we estimate the relevant timescales and their sensitivity to microphysics. Nevertheless, we show that a quadrupole component whose pattern speed differs from the observed spin is shifted, or smeared, over a finite frequency band. Single-template or narrowband upper limits therefore constrain only the quadrupole contribution lying inside the searched frequency window, not necessarily the full frequency-integrated quadrupole. Using simple models, we quantify this spectral redistribution over finite observation windows and discuss its implications for continuous-wave searches.

title: Generation of isolated attosecond soft x-ray pulses using a nondispersive inverse Cherenkov dielectric laser modulator
CRIMSONS: An online tool for modeling chemical enrichment with stochastic initial mass function sampling
abstract: Chemical enrichment is a universal process shaped by several interconnected factors, including stellar feedback, the nature of chemical polluters, and the underlying distribution of stellar masses. Three key ingredients are often difficult to treat simultaneously in chemical-evolution models: the stochastic sampling of the stellar initial mass function (IMF), uncertainties in stellar nucleosynthesis yields, and pre-enrichment from primordial Population III (Pop III) stars. In low star formation rate environments (SFR ≲ 10 −3 M ⊙ yr −1 ), incomplete IMF sampling makes enrichment sensitive to the random presence or absence of massive supernova progenitors. Here, we present CRIMSONS , the first online tool specifically designed to model chemical enrichment while self-consistently incorporating these three ingredients. The framework allows users to explore different IMFs, stellar population masses, and metallicities and multiple stellar yield sets. It follows the evolution of individual stars and tracks 30 elements (H–Zn), including contributions from supernovae, asymptotic giant branch stars, and Type Ia supernovae. The current implementation adopts a closed-box framework, neglecting gas flows and spatial mixing, thus providing a controlled setup to isolate the effects of IMF sampling, stellar yields, and Pop III pre-enrichment. With CRIMSONS , we show that incomplete IMF sampling produces a large (≥1 dex) abundance scatter, particularly in low-mass stellar populations. Different yield prescriptions introduce element-dependent variations, while some abundance ratios remain comparatively robust across models. Finally, comparison between models including primordial enrichment and those adopting only a metallicity floor showed that Pop III pre-enrichment can significantly affect subsequent chemical evolution. CRIMSONS therefore provides a controlled framework for quantifying the relative impact of stochastic IMF sampling, nucleosynthetic uncertainties, and primordial pre-enrichment on predicted abundance patterns.

title: Reinforcement Learning in High-Energy Physics: A Survey from Accelerator Control to Theory Exploration
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm in which an agent learns a decision-making policy by interacting with an environment, guided by a scalar reward rather than explicit supervision. Supervised and unsupervised learning have become indispensable tools in high-energy physics (HEP), but they learn from fixed datasets, whereas many HEP tasks are closed-loop decisions: the data an algorithm observes depend on its choices, the feedback is sparse or delayed, and the objective is often measured on a real machine or in a stochastic simulation, not by a differentiable model. This survey reviews the application of RL to such tasks: accelerator control and feedback, data quality monitoring, jet grooming, clustering, and representation, charged particle tracking, beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and formal quantum field theory computation. It provides a self-contained introduction to the underlying RL methods, from model-free and model-based to multi-agent, offline, inverse, and bandit approaches, reviews each domain against its traditional methods, and summarizes the head-to-head comparisons. The applications range from policies deployed on real accelerators and evaluated on recorded collision data to exploratory studies in formal theory. RL is most advantageous for repeated tasks with a fast simulator, decisions inside fast control loops, operation under faults and corrupted measurements, physics-based rewards in place of labels, and sequential discrete constructions with a reusable policy, while Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and differentiable methods remain competitive elsewhere. We conclude with the open challenges that recur across domains, including reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety, the lack of shared benchmarks, and the statistical validity of policy-driven decisions.

title: Entropy-based classification of core-collapse supernova gravitational waves for nuclear equation-of-state inference
abstract: Gravitational waves from core-collapse supernovae provide a unique probe of the physical processes occurring during stellar collapse and of the properties of dense nuclear matter. In this work we investigate the classification of supernova gravitational-wave signals associated with different nuclear equations of state using an entropy-based machine learning framework. The analysis combines signal decomposition, feature extraction, and feature selection techniques to identify informative characteristics of the waveforms and distinguish between different equation of state models. We evaluate the performance of several machine learning classifiers using a compact set of selected features and assess their robustness in the presence of detector noise. We find that entropy-based representations capture the underlying differences between waveform classes and enable accurate classification while maintaining better performance compared to raw data under noisy conditions. These results demonstrate the potential of complexity-based feature extraction as an efficient and interpretable approach for gravitational wave studies of core-collapse supernovae.

title: Spatiotemporal analysis of detached plasma response to electron beam injection using laser Thomson scattering
abstract: Abstract Transient heat loads like Edge Localized Modes (ELMs) can degrade detached plasmas that are essential for reducing divertor heat fluxes in future fusion reactors. To investigate the response of detached plasmas to transient electron energy deposition, a pulsed electron beam was injected into a detached helium plasma in the linear plasma device NAGDIS-II. Spatiotemporal evolutions of electron temperature and density were measured using laser Thomson scattering synchronized with the beam injection with high-temporal resolution. Despite the small beam source diameter (2 mm), significant changes in plasma parameters extended over a wide radial range (> 15 mm). The electron beam rapidly increased the electron temperature near the plasma center, resulting in a local transition from a recombining plasma to an ionizing plasma. In contrast, the electron density exhibited a slower temporal evolution, suggesting different underlying mechanisms governing temperature and density responses. The measured spatiotemporal plasma parameters were further analyzed using a collisional-radiative model and reproduced previously observed line-integrated emission dynamics. These results demonstrate that localized electron energy deposition can induce a global response in detached plasmas and provide new insight into the stability and dynamic behavior of detached plasmas subjected to transient energy loads.

title: Single-pass stochastic cooling for electron microscopy
abstract: Scientific applications of free electrons, such as in electron microscopes and particle accelerators, are limited by the brightness of available electron sources. Accelerators can use phase space cooling to surpass these source limitations, whereas electron microscopes can only rely on particle filtering to increase beam coherence at the cost of reduced brightness. We show that strong electron-light coupling in nanophotonic structures makes it possible to achieve single-pass stochastic cooling inside an electron microscope for a lossless improvement of longitudinal emittance. This approach is laser-free and compatible with normal CW operation of electron microscopes. We derive a fully quantum mechanical model of stochastic cooling valid in the strong coupling regime, finding an analytic asymptotic formula for the optimal cooled energy spread $\sigma_{E_f}\simeq0.88(\hbar\omega)^{2/3}\sigma_{E_0}^{1/3}$, with $\hbar \omega$ the cooling photon energy and $\sigma_{E_0}$ the initial energy spread. Numerical simulations confirm that the energy spread reduction is reflected in an increase in the purity of the electron's quantum state and a reduction of the longitudinal phase space area. Our work paves a path towards even brighter beams for electron microscopy, promising higher image quality, enhanced spectral resolution, and a route to reaching fundamental quantum limits on electron beam phase space area.

title: LH$\mu$C Concept: Energy-Frontier Antimuon-Proton Collisions at CERN
abstract: The concept of the LH$\mu$C, an energy-frontier antimuon-proton collider based on the HL-LHC, is presented. After recalling why energy-frontier lepton-hadron colliders are indispensable as QCD explorers and reviewing the history of muon-proton collider proposals, two ways of realising $\mu p$ collisions at the LHC are compared: with muon-collider beams and with ultra-cold $\mu^+$ beams as proposed for $\mu$TRISTAN. For the latter, a $\mu$TRISTAN-type booster and the re-use of the LHeC energy-recovery-linac tunnel are discussed; colliding 1 TeV antimuons with 7 TeV protons gives $\sqrt{s}=5.3$ TeV and peak luminosities of $8.8\times10^{33}$ and $7.2\times10^{33}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, respectively. The detector concept and the physics potential, including searches for colour-octet muons and R-parity-violating squarks, are discussed together with the main challenges.

title: Comments on the paper "Eliminating beam-induced depolarizing effects in the hydrogen jet target for high-precision proton beam polarimetry at the Electron-Ion Collider"
abstract: A critical review of the methodology used in F. Rathmann et al., Phys. Rev. Accel. Beams 29, 021001 (2026), to evaluate beam-induced depolarization of the Atomic Polarized Hydrogen Gas Jet (HJET) target at the Electron--Ion Collider (EIC) is presented. It is shown that several key assumptions underlying that analysis -- including the introduction of a photon emission threshold, the application of Fermi's Golden Rule to coherent hyperfine transitions, the interpretation of power broadening as a physical linewidth increase, and the treatment of spatial magnetic fields -- are either incorrect or internally inconsistent. As a consequence, the predicted large depolarization effects are demonstrated to be artifacts of the adopted methodology rather than genuine physical phenomena. A consistent quantum-mechanical treatment based on the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation shows that beam-induced depolarization probabilities at the EIC are negligibly small.

title: A Collapsar-Disk Origin for GW190814
abstract: GW190814 was a remarkable gravitational-wave (GW) event: a merger between a $23 M_\odot$ black hole (BH) and a $2.6\,M_\odot$ compact object, with an extreme mass ratio that is difficult to reproduce through standard isolated-binary or dynamical formation channels. Recent work has shown that neutrino-cooled collapsar disks can become gravitationally unstable and fragment, producing neutron stars (NSs) or low-mass BHs in orbit around the newly formed central BH. These fragments may subsequently interact, scatter, merge with one another, or inspiral into the central remnant. We explore the possibility that GW190814 originated from such a collapsar-disk fragment merging with the central BH. A key prediction of this scenario is a temporal association with a stripped-envelope supernova preceding the GW event, and we identify the Type Ib supernova candidate SN2019npv, which occurred inside the GW190814 credible volume approximately 60 days before coalescence, as a possible electromagnetic precursor. Although this delay is too long for a conventional kilonova counterpart, we show that three-body interactions among disk fragments can excite some compact objects to wide orbits and produce merger delays of weeks to months. While GW190814 itself was not expected to produce detectable tidal-disruption-powered emission, future delayed mergers in this channel could generate luminous transients through either reprocessed kilonova heating or shocks driven as merger ejecta collide with the preceding supernova ejecta. Finally, treating SN2019npv as the electromagnetic counterpart makes GW190814 a bright standard siren and yields $H_{0} = 71.1^{+9.3}_{-7.5} km s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}$.

title: Quantum Correlations Between Two Giant Dipole Resonances in Ultra-Peripheral Collisions
abstract: Mutual Coulomb dissociation in ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions is dominated by Giant Dipole Resonance (GDR) excitation, whose subsequent decays produce forward neutrons. Standard descriptions treat the two GDRs excited in opposite nuclei as statistically independent, leading primarily to a quadrupolar azimuthal correlation determined by the common photon-polarization axis. In this work, we investigate the possibility that the two GDRs are instead prepared with a correlated quantum phase during the overlap of the electromagnetic pulses. We develop a phase-sensitive GDR decay model and implement it in a modified version of the \texttt{$n_{0}^{0}n$} Monte Carlo generator, allowing a quantitative comparison among three competing mechanisms: the weak dipolar modulation from electromagnetic recoil, the quadrupolar correlation from independent polarized GDR decays, and the phase-sensitive dipolar modulation associated with the proposed phase-lock scenario. For neutron pairs with small relative emission-time differences, the correlated-phase scenario produces a pronounced first-harmonic modulation in the two-neutron relative-azimuth distribution. Averaging over all relative emission times substantially reduces this modulation. Within the adopted energy-dependent angular model, the time-selected dipolar coefficient increases in magnitude with pair-mean neutron kinetic energy. These results identify neutron relative-azimuth correlations and their energy dependence as experimentally accessible observables for probing quantum phase correlations between the two GDR excitations. Such phase-sensitive correlations could also provide a basis for future tests of quantum entanglement between spatially separated GDR excitations at RHIC and the LHC.

title: Thermal Festina Lente
abstract: According to the Festina Lente bound, particles charged under a $U(1)$ gauge field cannot be too light. Otherwise, the largest charged black holes of de Sitter space would discharge in a way that leads to a crunching singularity in violation of cosmic censorship. The Festina Lente bound has previously been extended to also include a background of thermal radiation, but where vacuum energy still dominates cosmic evolution, which imposes a maximal temperature $T\leq T_{\max}=(cV/\sigma)^{1/4}$. We extend this analysis by accounting for thermal enhancement of the discharge process and making the analysis more quantitative. The result is a bound $m\gtrsim\ell (cV/\sigma)^{1/4}$ on the masses of charged particles. Here, $\ell$ is a term that depends logarithmically on the gauge coupling and particle charge. At weak coupling this leads to a significantly stronger constraint than the $\sqrt{gq}$ scaling of the original Festina Lente bound. As a result, the present vacuum energy requires every particle of charge $10^{-26}\lesssim gq\lesssim e$ to be heavier than $0.03$--$0.2$ eV, provided its gauge boson is lighter than the Hubble scale. An unbroken gauged $B-L$ with Dirac neutrinos gives $m_{\nu,{\rm lightest}}\gtrsim10$--$43$ meV for $10^{-29}\lesssim g_{B-L}\lesssim10^{-24}$, in tension with the DESI DR2 limit once $g_{B-L}\gtrsim7\times10^{-28}$. The same limit bounds a neutrino millicharge to $\epsilon_\nu\lesssim2\times10^{-27}$. We also revisit the Standard Model effective field theory constraints from the electroweak phase transition. During slow-roll inflation the Standard Model electron violates the bound over the whole range of Hubble rates allowed by the CMB tensor limit and by nucleosynthesis, unless the photon is Higgsed, its coupling is suppressed, or one considers very fine-tuned versions of Higgs inflation.

title: SensOFormer: Foundation Models for Particle Accelerators
abstract: Large-scale scientific facilities, such as particle accelerators, are complex systems composed of thousands of interacting components that must operate collectively to support diagnostics and control, and ensure safe, reliable operation. These facilities rely on extensive sensor networks that generate large volumes of heterogeneous, incomplete, and noisy telemetry, often sampled at different rates across subsystems. In this paper, we adopt the foundation-model paradigm to learn general-purpose sensor representations from historical accelerator data through self-supervised pretraining. We introduce SensOFormer, a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder architecture designed to handle variable sensor sets, accommodate heterogeneous sampling rates, and learn robust representations from noisy measurements. The model is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets and transferred to downstream tasks, including missing-data imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification, and fault identification. Through extensive evaluations and comparisons, we demonstrate that a single self-supervised model can learn reusable representations for diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/sensoformer.

title: OPALX: A performance-portable framework for particle accelerator simulations
abstract: Accurate charged-particle beam simulations require self-consistent collective fields and realistic accelerator models, while their computational cost motivates efficient use of heterogeneous computing systems. We present OPALX, a performance-portable accelerator simulation framework that builds on the beam-dynamics capabilities of OPAL. Its modular architecture uses the Independent Parallel Particle Layer (IPPL) and Kokkos to support distributed-memory execution on multicore CPUs and GPUs from a common codebase. The framework combines relativistic particle tracking with prescribed accelerator fields, particle-in-cell space charge calculations, and spin tracking. We describe the physical and numerical models and their integration into the simulation workflow. The implementation is assessed using disorder-induced heating and frozen-spin test cases, together with comparisons of spin evolution with G4Beamline and beam transport with TraceWin. A three-dimensional space charge benchmark evaluates throughput on CPU and GPU systems, reaching approximately $10^9$ macroparticles per second on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU for this benchmark. These results provide initial verification of the implemented models and demonstrate CPU and GPU execution of self-consistent space charge calculations. OPALX provides a common foundation for extending accelerator models and numerical methods across heterogeneous computing platforms.

title: Numerical Study of Two-Frequency Heating in ECR Ion Source
abstract: The two-frequency heating (TFH) method is widely used to improve the performance of electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) ion sources, yet its physical mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. In this work, the TFH regime in the DECRIS-PM ECR ion source is studied numerically using the NAM-ECRIS code. Single-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz (500 W) is compared to two-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz and 13 GHz (450 W + 50 W) at equal total power. It is found that while the global plasma parameters remain largely unchanged, the peak density of highly anisotropic electrons (E > 1 keV, Vperp/Vlong > 10) decreases by ~20% and their distribution broadens radially in the TFH regime. This reduction in electron anisotropy is attributed to the randomizing effect of the lower-frequency wave on electron gyromotion, which suppresses plasma micro-instabilities and leads to improved ion production.

title: Inverse modelling of a laser-plasma accelerator
abstract: The electron beams of a laser-plasma accelerator depend non-linearly on the laser and gas settings. This dependence is explored using particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations, and machine-learning models trained on these simulations predict the beam from the settings. Here we address the reverse problem: given a measured beam, which settings produced it? We infer three of them: the gas pressure $p\_1$, the normalised vector potential $a\_0$ and the nitrogen concentration $c\_{N\_2}$. The solution is not guaranteed to be unique. We train an ensemble of mixture density networks that, for each beam, output several possible sets of settings with their probabilities and uncertainties, and test them on simulated beams with realistic measurement noise. On average, the predictions are accurate ($R^2 = 0.91$), yet for about two-thirds of the beams the inferred distribution has two competing solutions. These share nearly the same value of $a\_0^2 p\_1$, which controls how strongly the laser focuses itself in the plasma and, in earlier PALLAS studies, when electrons start to be injected. Keeping this quantity fixed gives beams that are practically indistinguishable with realistic diagnostics. A forward model used as a check removes unphysical solutions but cannot choose between the two plausible ones. We then test two ways to resolve the ambiguity. Adding the full electron energy spectrum improves the mean prediction ($R^2 = 0.94$), mostly through $a\_0$. It changes the weights of the two solutions but does not move them. A second measurement at a deliberately different plasma density is more effective. In paired PIC simulations, it reduces the error on $a\_0$ by a factor of 2.6, whereas repeating the measurement at the same density brings almost no gain.

title: Improvement of Heat-Treated Niobium Surface by In-situ Plasma Treatment Applied to Superconducting RF Resonator
abstract: A specific heat treatment at 300 C, named medium-temperature baking (Mid-T baking) is applied to superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerating cavities to improve the quality factor (Qo) at medium accelerating fields (10 to 20 MV/m). This treatment is very successful when done properly as it can reduce by almost a factor of two the power dissipations in this field range. However, surface contamination can lead to the degradation of Qo instead. Plasma-based surface treatment provides an effective approach to eliminate contaminants from the Niobium surface. In this study an insitu plasma cleaning process with argon containing 10 % O2 was performed to remove hydrocarbons from Niobium surface. The treatment was applied before and after a heat treatment at 500 C under ultra-high vacuum conditions (Mid-T baking). Changes in chemical speciation and oxide layer alteration induced by plasma processing were analyzed using insitu X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and exsitu scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The results show that plasma treatment modifies the composition of Niobium oxides, converting a Nb2O5 layer into NbO2. Furthermore, a plasma treatment before Mid-T baking helps reduce unstable oxides such as NbxO and significantly increases the proportion of metallic Niobium at the surface. The Niobium sample treated by plasma prior to Mid-T baking showed a 53 % reduction in carbide formation. Moreover, the C1s component attributed to NbC bonds shifts toward lower binding energy, indicating the formation of a more metallic NbC phase. Whereas without plasma treatment, the higher binding energy component observed after Mid T baking is consistent with Nb2C.

title: Impact of Rapid Acceleration on Beam Dynamics in the Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons of a Muon Collider
abstract: Circular muon colliders offer a promising route to multi-TeV centre-of-mass energies with high luminosity. The baseline design for the high-energy complex includes a chain of four Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons (RCSs) accelerating the beam from \qty{63}{\GeV} to \qty{5}{\TeV}. The chain combines a conventional synchrotron with three hybrid synchrotrons, which use fixed-field superconducting dipoles and rapidly ramped normal-conducting dipoles. The short muon lifetime (\qty{2.2}{\micro\second} in the rest frame) imposes stringent constraints on the acceleration process: achieving the target luminosity requires a muon survival rate of up to \qty{70}{\percent} throughout the acceleration chain, with the full acceleration completed in approximately \qty{10}{\milli\second}. These demanding acceleration conditions raise several beam-dynamics challenges, investigated in this work. First, the impact of the RF cavity distribution on transverse emittance growth is studied. Second, the mismatch between the discretely increasing beam energy and the continuously ramped fields of the pulsed dipoles and quadrupoles is modelled analytically, and its impact is evaluated through tracking simulations. Finally, the sensitivity of the beam trajectory, optical functions, and emittance growth to magnetic-field ramp jitter is assessed.

title: Extending the Pulsar radio population through Quantum Vacuum Cherenkov Emission
abstract: The presence of some radio pulsars within and below the so-called ``death valley'' in the $P$--$\dot{P}$ diagram challenges the standard pair-cascade models based on curvature radiation (CR) and resonant inverse Compton scattering (RICS) in neutron star polar caps. We show that Cherenkov radiation from the quantum vacuum, a strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) phenomenon enabled by vacuum polarization, constitutes a distinct pair-creation channel within the vacuum gap model. Within this model, the acceleration length scale for Cherenkov photon emission and the subsequent photon mean free path are sufficiently short to ensure rapid conversion into $e^+e^-$ pairs. This process acts as a complementary pair-creation channel, remaining viable even in regimes where classical mechanisms become heavily suppressed. This leads to a new set of death lines in the $P$--$\dot{P}$ diagram that partially overlap with and extend beyond the CR and RICS death valleys, enlarging the viable parameter space for radio-emitting neutron stars. The result provides a physical basis for coherent radio emission from long-period neutron stars previously considered inactive, and offers a new window for testing non-linear QED with next-generation radio facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array.

title: Bayesian optimization of longitudinally aligned CNT targets for 800 nm laser wakefield acceleration in the bubble regime
abstract: Laser wakefield acceleration (LWFA) in solid-density plasmas can reach accelerating gradients in the TeV/m range, well above those of gaseous media, provided the driver is matched to the plasma. In nanostructured solids, this matching can be achieved by controlling the spacing between the nanostructures to reduce the effective density, enabling infrared pulses to excite wakefields in the bubble regime. Following numerical demonstrations with carbon nanotube (CNT) bundles on concentric cylindrical shells, a simpler, experimentally more accessible longitudinally aligned CNT (LA-CNT) target is investigated here, with the bundles on a triangular lattice within a square cross section and an optional central aperture. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations are coupled with Bayesian optimization to vary the effective density, target length, bundle radius and aperture radius for a fixed 100 mJ, few-cycle, 800 nm laser pulse, maximizing the laser-to-beam energy conversion efficiency for electrons above 20 MeV. With the aperture radius constrained to at least 0.5 $\mu$m, the best target operates in the bubble regime and reaches an efficiency of 24.6%, delivering a 673 pC bunch with a mean energy of 36.6 MeV and a quasi-monoenergetic peak near 46 MeV, against 19% for the concentric-shell target under identical conditions. When the aperture is allowed to vanish, the optimization converges to denser and shorter targets, the efficiency peaks at 25.8%, and the best configurations deliver a higher charge at the cost of a lower peak energy and about 50% larger divergence; aperture-free targets among them retain a mean efficiency of 24.1%. The optimized targets are robust to random bundle displacements that preserve the effective density. By eliminating the need to pattern a micrometre-scale opening, aperture-free targets may facilitate proof-of-principle experiments on solid-state LWFA.

title: Strong vertex $N N \rho$ in dense medium
abstract: We investigate the strong coupling form factors associated with the $NN\rho$ interaction vertex in nuclear matter using the QCD sum rule framework. These form factors are calculated incorporating the in-medium modifications of the relevant condensates and operators into the operator product expansion (OPE) for the first time. We analyze the behavior of the strong form factors as functions of the momentum transfer squared and density of medium and evaluate the corresponding strong couplings at the on-shell point of the $\rho$ meson at nuclear saturation density. Then we extend the analyses to get information at higher densities. Our results provide complementary information on the in-medium $NN\rho$ interaction and may be useful for phenomenological, experimental and observational studies of dense hadronic matter.

title: Signatures of quark matter from neutron star mass-radius curve
abstract: Signatures of the presence of quark matter inside neutron stars are obtained from the analysis of more than 250,000 mass-radius curves that describe nucleonic, hyperonic and hybrid stars, based on five different hadronic relativistic mean-field models and four different descriptions of quark matter. A radius maximum occurring above $1.7\,M_\odot$ strongly favors quark matter inside the star. A second criterion identifying the presence of quark matter is $X>-0.2$km, where X=[R(2.0)-R(1.6)]-[R(1.6)-R(1.4)] is obtained from the radius of stars with 2.0, 1.6 and 1.4 $M_\odot$. It is also shown that most of the hyperonic stars have a radius maximum that peaks around 1.5$M_\odot$ and compactness below 0.27 for the maximum-mass configuration, while for the nucleonic stars that have a radius maximum, this peaks below 1.3$M_\odot$ and the compactness of the maximum-mass configuration lies above 0.26.

title: Signatures of Novikov-Thorne accretion disks around rotating black holes in semiclassical gravity with trace anomaly
abstract: Abstract Semiclassical gravity provides a promising framework to address the black hole singularity problem through quantum backreaction characterized by a coupling parameter, making it essential to thoroughly explore the accretion properties around such objects. In this paper, within the framework of semiclassical gravity with type-A trace anomaly, we investigate the thermal radiative signatures of Novikov-Thorne accretion disks around rotating black holes across diverse parameter spaces, focusing on the energy flux density, temperature profile, and thermal luminosity. Our findings demonstrate that the introduction of a positive coupling parameter suppresses disk emission, leading to lower peak values of both energy flux density and temperature, as well as lower peak values and corresponding peak frequencies in thermal luminosity compared to their Kerr counterparts in general relativity. In particular, this discrepancy becomes remarkably pronounced when the black hole possesses a high spin. Mechanistically, increasing the coupling parameter reinforces the effective gravitational field strength of the central compact object, which pushes the equatorial stable circular orbits outward and increases the specific energy of the orbiting matter, thereby reducing the radiative efficiency and weakening the overall disk emission. This suppression mechanism offers a potential astrophysical window to distinguish semiclassical gravity from general relativity and to place observational constraints on the coupling parameter via thermal disk spectra.

title: Perfect crystal neutron loop cavity
abstract: Coherent control of neutrons via Bragg diffraction forms the foundation of perfect crystal neutron interferometry, facilitating both fundamental tests of quantum mechanics and applications in quantum information science. In cavity geometries, perfect crystals enable neutron confinement and have been employed in precision measurements of spin-orbit interactions and for neutron electric dipole moment (nEDM) searches. However, in these conventional configurations, neutrons undergo a single pass through the crystal geometry, placing a physical constraint on both crystal and in-flight interaction times and measurement sensitivity. In this work, we introduce a neutron loop cavity that coherently recirculates neutrons through repeated Bragg reflections between perfect silicon crystal blades. This structure is predicted to achieve a neutron unitary survival probability of ∼ 64 % for 10 000 Bragg reflections, corresponding to confinement times on the order of seconds. We propose a Schwinger interaction measurement that achieves a π spin rotation in 800 Bragg reflections, representing more than a tenfold improvement in sensitivity over recent measurements. Further applications include nEDM searches targeting the 10 − 27 e cm scale, as well as experimental tests of neutron parity violation, the neutron lifetime, and the quantum Zeno effect with neutrons.

title: New Scaling Relations for Nucleons in Three-Nucleon Short-Range Correlations
abstract: The search for three nucleon short range correlations~(3N- SRCs) in nuclei is one of the intensive areas of research in high density nuclear physics. It is in part motivated by the prediction of the above two-solar mass neutron stars based on 3N short-range forces and the subsequent observation of such stars. The 3N-SRCs serve as a "laboratory" for probing the dynamics of largely unknown irreducible 3N-forces. However, the identification of 3N-SRCs in high energy nuclear processes is still elusive making the prospects of their investigation problematic. In this work we introduced new dynamical parameters for 2N- and 3N- SRCs, $\beta_{2N}$ and $\beta_{3N}$ respectively, which characterize the strength of SRCs beyond combinatorial counting of nucleons in SRCs. For 2N-SRCs the introduction of $\beta_{2N}$ parameter resulted in a previously known and experimentally verified relation for proton and neutron momentum distributions in 2N-SRCS. For 3N-SRCs the $\beta_{3N}$ parameter allowed to factorize momentum distributions of nucleons in the correlation resulting in a prediction of a new scaling relation between proton and neutron momentum distributions in 3N SRCs. This relation, if valid gives a new venue for identification of 3N-SRCs in electro-nuclear processes. Even though the obtained scaling relation is relevant in the relativistic domain, the possibility of separating center of mass motion of SRCs on the light-front allows to check the validity of predicted scaling using non-relativistic ab-initio wave functions. We found surprisingly reasonable confirmation of our prediction analyzing ab-initio wave functions of nuclei in the range $3\le A\le 12$. This indicates the robustness of the scaling relation and opens up a new direction in searching for 3N-SRCs experimentally.

title: Mass and angular momentum assessement of the neutron star XTEJ 1807-294 using X-ray triplets
abstract: The X-ray power-density spectrum of the accreting millisecond pulsar XTEJ 1807-294 contains several triplets of simultaneously observed quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs): a lower and a upper kHz QPOs and a low-frequency QPO. This fact allows us to assess the mass and the specific angular momentum of the central neutron star. We also apply an error propagation formula to obtain interval estimates of the parameters of the star. The calculations are repeated with several different models for the kHz QPOs. The degree of consistency of the bounds obtained with the different triplets may provide information for the viability of the used models.

title: Lightest and heaviest nuclei as keys to the origin of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays
abstract: The origin of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has been a long-standing mystery. A unique feature of UHECRs originating in binary neutron star mergers (BNSMs) is two distinct populations of light elements -- those directly accelerated in the jets, and photo-disintegration products of massive nuclei accelerated in the bulk outflow. We show that Pierre Auger Observatory spectrum and composition data confirm the existence of the predicted two populations at $\geq \!7.2\sigma$ significance, having rigidity ($R\equiv E/Ze$) cutoffs agreeing with prior estimates. The data also favor 5-10% of UHECRs originating as r-process nuclei, a signature of a BNSM origin. Our results provide strong evidence that UHECRs are produced by merging neutron stars, and show how UHECRs and UHE-neutrinos elucidate otherwise inaccessible aspects of neutron star mergers.

title: Higher-Order Symmetry Energy Effects on the Properties of Neutron Stars
abstract: We study the effects of the symmetry-energy curvature $K_{\rm sym}$ on the equation of state (EoS) and neutron-star properties within the relativistic mean-field (RMF) framework. We construct controlled families of RMF parametrizations based on the TM1 and IUFSU models by varying $K_{\rm sym}$ while keeping the symmetry energy $J$ and its slope $L$ fixed at saturation density. We find that, although a larger $K_{\rm sym}$ leads to a lower symmetry energy at suprasaturation densities and a reduced proton fraction in $\beta$-equilibrated matter, it results in a stiffer EoS and a higher sound speed. The maximum neutron-star mass is weakly affected, whereas the canonical radius $R_{1.4}$ exhibits a nearly linear dependence on $K_{\rm sym}$.

title: Global and crustal properties of neutron stars
abstract: We investigate how the treatment of the neutron star crust affects both the global properties of the star and the properties of the crust itself. Three approaches are compared: a direct connection between a fixed crust and the core equation of state (EOS), a smooth crossover between them, and a unified EOS in which the crust is computed within a compressible liquid-drop model with the same nuclear empirical parameters of the relativistic mean-field model used for the core. For each approach, we consider four values of the symmetry energy slope, $44 \le L \le 92$ MeV. For a $1.4\,M_\odot$ star, some global properties are weakly to moderately affected: the radius and the moment of inertia agree within 1\% among the three approaches. On the other hand, the tidal deformability obtained with the direct connection is up to 21\% lower than the unified one for $L = 92$ MeV. A much larger contrast comes from the crustal properties. Relative to the unified EOS, the direct connection yields a crust that is 15--36\% thinner, 6--12 times less massive, and that carries a fraction of the total moment of inertia 5--8 times smaller (0.3--1.1\% instead of 2.8--6.2\%). The differences between crust treatments are thus comparable to or larger than those arising from variations in $L$ for crustal properties, while they remain subleading for global ones.

title: Effects of Competing Reactions on $^{59}\mathrm{Cu}$ and $^{63}\mathrm{Ga}$ on Abundance Distributions in Type I X-Ray Bursts
abstract: The composition of X-ray burst ashes affects the thermal transport properties of the neutron star crust, as well as heating and cooling through weak interaction processes. Reaction-rate uncertainties can produce secondary peaks separated from the main peak in final abundance distributions. Using STARLIB reaction rates and their temperature-dependent uncertainties in the K04 one-zone post-processing model, we combine four sets of Monte Carlo calculations with XGBoost classification, SHAP analysis, and reaction-flow analysis to investigate the origins of these secondary peaks. We find that the competing $(p,\alpha)$ and $(p,\gamma)$ reaction pairs on $^{59}\mathrm{Cu}$ and $^{63}\mathrm{Ga}$ are primarily responsible for secondary peaks outside the central 68\% confidence interval in all 44 isotopes examined. Fixing both pairs at their median rates reduces the fractions of samples in the secondary-peak regions by 96\%--100\%, while the bounds of the central 68\% interval remain largely unchanged for most mass numbers. The $^{59}\mathrm{Cu}$ pair has the larger effect. Enhanced recycling limits the supply of material to heavier isotopes and accelerates proton consumption, while earlier proton exhaustion further suppresses subsequent proton captures. These changes alter the balance between isotope production and destruction, leading to high- or low-abundance secondary peaks over a broad mass range beyond the Ni--Cu and Zn--Ga cycles. These results identify $^{59}\mathrm{Cu}(p,\gamma)^{60}\mathrm{Zn}$ and the two competing channels on $^{63}\mathrm{Ga}$ as priorities for further nuclear-physics constraints to improve XRB abundance predictions.

title: DBI Softens Stiff-Phase Gravitational-Wave Spectra
abstract: We investigate the effect of non-canonical kinetic terms on the present-day density spectrum of primordial gravitational waves (GWs), by considering the dynamics of a scalar field governed by the Dirac--Born--Infeld (DBI) action and a runaway potential. The field, responsible for a period of inflation, subsequently enters a kinetically dominated regime, where the DBI structure reduces the equation-of-state parameter relative to the canonical kination result $w=1$, thereby softening the blue tilt of the GW spectrum. Simultaneously, the energy density of the field redshifts at a slower rate, delaying radiation domination and prolonging the stiff phase. The interplay between these two effects can lead to a potentially observable GW signal that would otherwise remain beyond the reach of future experiments in the canonical case. We test our predictions by numerically solving the background and perturbations, from inflation until radiation domination, and find viable parameter space compatible with cosmic microwave background and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis constraints.

title: A concordance model of neutron star kicks
abstract: Neutron stars (NSs) receive natal kicks during supernovae that affect their survival in binaries and motion through the Galaxy. The global distribution of these kick velocities across the NS population remains uncertain. Here, we combine the orbital properties and birth rates of Gaia NS and Be+NS binaries with velocity constraints from young isolated pulsars to construct a concordance model of NS natal kicks. We find that all three populations can be jointly described by a shared bimodal kick distribution. The low-velocity component follows a lognormal distribution with $\mu_{\ln v}=1.87^{+0.65}_{-0.53}$ and $\sigma_{\ln v}=0.55^{+0.85}_{-0.44}$, corresponding to a median speed of $6.5^{+5.9}_{-2.7}~{\rm km~s^{-1}}$. The high-velocity component is consistent with the distribution inferred from young pulsars, which peaks near $200~{\rm km~s^{-1}}$. The low-velocity component contributes only $\sim10\%$ of all NS births, but produces most Gaia NS binaries and roughly half of Be+NS binaries. The same model predicts systemic recoil velocities consistent with the observed kinematics of Gaia NSs, Be+NS binaries, and NS low-mass X-ray binaries. For Gaia NSs, whose formation history remains unknown, we use this kick distribution to constrain their progenitors. We favor pre-supernova binaries containing intermediate-mass stripped stars with $\sim1~{\rm M_\odot}$ companions in au-scale orbits, and predict $\sim300$ such binaries in the Milky Way today, $\sim40$ in the LMC, and $\sim30$ in the SMC. Finally, we consider the implications of these kicks for NSs in hierarchical triples. We find that 2-10$\%$ of Gaia NS triples and 3-23$\%$ of Be+NS triples retain their tertiary after the supernova. Overall, our results suggest that a shared natal kick law can account for isolated pulsars and surviving NS binaries, where most NSs receive large kicks and low kicks are common among surviving binaries.

title: Hydrodynamic assessment of direct-drive inertial confinement fusion with mixed 2ω−3ω lasers
abstract: Ablation with mixed 2ω–3ω lasers is investigated as a drive strategy for direct-drive inertial confinement fusion, balancing hydrodynamic drive efficiency, ablative stabilization, and facility-level energy constraints. One-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of planar CH targets are performed with the FLASH code [Fryxell et al., Astrophys. J., Suppl. Ser. 131, 273 (2000)], varying the total incident intensity from 100 to 1600 TW/cm2 and the 3ω intensity fraction f3ω from 0 to 100%. Increasing f3ω raises the ablation pressure and the ablation velocity, lowers the maximum linear Rayleigh–Taylor instability (RTI) gain evaluated with a Takabe-type model, and reduces the target-incident energy required to accelerate a foil to 300 km/s, because the 3ω light deposits its energy closer to the dense ablation region and enhances conductive heat transport toward the ablation front. When representative frequency-conversion efficiencies are folded into the energy budget, the required fundamental-frequency (1ω) energy becomes non-monotonic in f3ω at high intensity, with an interior minimum near f3ω≈20%–30% lying below both single-color drives. Because the energy landscape around this minimum is shallow, f3ω can be raised moderately above it to strengthen RTI stabilization and widen the sub-threshold window for two-plasmon decay at a 1ω energy cost of only a few percent. These results identify f3ω≈30%–50% as a preferred operating window and establish the wavelength-mixing ratio as an additional design degree of freedom for direct-drive target optimization.

title: Source shapes in coordinate and momentum space in $\sqrt{s_\text{NN}}$ = 200 GeV Au+Au collisions
abstract: In high-energy heavy-ion physics, femtoscopy aims to explore and understand the space-time characteristics of the collisions through investigating the correlation function of particle pairs. In recent years, experimental measurements have shown that the shape of the particle source function can be well described by the L\'evy distribution, motivating further phenomenological studies. In this work, we perform a three-dimensional analysis of the source shapes for different particle-pair types in $\sqrt{s_\text{NN}}=200$ GeV Au+Au collisions generated with the EPOS event generator. In contrast to our previous analyses, where we fitted the one-dimensional projections of the pair distribution function, $D(\rho_j)$ ($j \in \{\text{out}, \text{side}, \text{long}\}$), now we reconstruct the three-dimensional $C(\boldsymbol{q})$ correlation function and fit it directly, as in experimental analyses. Furthermore, we now apply full three-dimensional fits instead of fitting the one-dimensional projections. We find that this approach results in smaller L\'evy index values, while the direction averaged L\'evy scale and the correlation strength remain largely unchanged, except for kaons. In the case of pions, the $\alpha$ values are closer to the PHENIX data, showing a good agreement above 20\% centrality.

title: Measuring the Neutron-Star Moment of Inertia using Nonlinear Orbital Variations from Lense-Thirring Precession
abstract: A future measurement of Lense-Thirring (LT) precession using a binary radio pulsar is expected to yield the pulsar's moment of inertia ($I_{\rm p}$). However, most of the known pulsar-binary systems expected to provide this opportunity will exhibit linear variations in the orbital elements, due to LT precession, that are difficult to separate from distance-dependent variations induced by other mechanisms. In this work, we demonstrate that the pulsar-timing signature of LT precession for an arbitrary orbital orientation produces nonlinear orbital variations after a sufficient amount of time; if detected, these nonlinear variations provide a means to constrain $I_{\rm p}$ without the need for independent measurements of orbital geometry or distance. We show through simulations that these nonlinear signatures are indeed detectable in pulsar-binary systems with an appropriate combination of timing precision and orbital geometry. Our simulations also show that nonlinear orbital variations from LT precession are expected to be detectable in PSR J1757$-$1854 and that its $I_{\rm p}$ can be constrained to precision as high as 10% by 2040 even without knowledge of distance.

title: Bayesian inference of the Landau parameter G ′ 0 from joint Gamow-Teller measurements
abstract: $G'_0$ is the leading-order Landau-Migdal parameter that characterizes the spin-isospin dependent nucleon-nucleon interaction. Consequently, the $G'_0$ is closely related to the Gamow-Teller resonance (GTR), the beta and double-beta decay rates of finite nuclei, the response of hot and dense nucleonic matter that modifies the neutrino-nucleon absorption rates in core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) and binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, and finally the critical density for pion condensation in neutron stars. In this letter, for the first time, we report the $G'_0$ with quantified uncertainty in the framework of Bayesian inference, using a self-consistent standard Skyrme Random Phase Approximation (RPA) model and joint constraints from experimental GTR measurements on $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$, $^{132}\mathrm{Sn}$, $^{90}\mathrm{Zr}$. Our extracted $G_0'$ at saturation density is $0.48\pm0.034$, which is close to the prediction of a few existing Skyrme models that consider spin-isospin observables but smaller than the traditional ones extracted from pion-exchange models. The reasons for this deviation, like the value of the nucleon effective mass $\frac{m^*}{m}$ and the density dependence of $G'_0$, are investigated. The density-dependent $G_0'$ values extracted in this work may guide the construction of new energy density functionals that aims to self-consistently describe the dense matter properties in the spin-isospin channel.

title: Decay spectroscopy of Tb 152 : A diagnostic component of the terbium theragnostic toolbox
abstract: Terbium-152, decaying by electron capture and β + emission to the ground and excited states in Gd 152 , shows potential for use in PET imaging as part of personalized cancer treatments. We report results of decay spectroscopy measurements, providing nuclear data necessary for medical use of this radionuclide. Sources of Tb 152 were prepared at CERN-ISOLDE by proton-induced spallation of a tantalum target, followed by on-line mass separation. The decay of these sources was measured at ILL Grenoble using the γ -ray coincidence spectrometer FIPPS and the PN1 electron- γ coincidence spectroscopy setup. We present an updated level scheme for the decay, comprising 751 γ -ray transitions placed to 200 excited states. Angular correlation analysis and conversion-electron spectroscopy provide spin-parity assignments to levels, multipolarity assignments to γ rays, and measurements of electric monopole transition strengths. A transition intensity balance of the resulting level scheme provides beta feeding intensities for each level, showing an 8.9% reduction in the positron emission probability and an increase of 4.5% in the γ -ray energy emitted per decay compared to the existing evaluated data for this decay.

title: Neutrino absorption in two-flavor color-superconducting quark matter
abstract: We calculate the absorption mean free paths of electron and muon neutrinos in two-flavor color-superconducting (2SC) quark matter in the density and temperature range that is relevant to binary neutron star mergers. We model the strong interaction between quarks using a Nambu–Jona-Lasinio model, performing calculations self-consistently in the mean-field approximation. Since the 2SC gap is large we restrict our analysis to the contribution of unpaired quarks. We find that at low temperatures absorption by a down quark ν + d → u + e − / μ − is kinematically not allowed, so absorption by a strange quark, ν + s → u + e − / μ − , dominates the mean free path. As temperature or neutrino energy rises, the d quark absorption channel becomes active, and the mean free path shrinks. We find that in equilibrated 2SC matter with an electron lepton fraction Y L e = 0.1 , the neutrinos form a degenerate gas with a mean free path of meters or less, independently of the temperature.

title: Multitask Gaussian process predictions of low-lying excitation observables and shell evolution near N , Z = 20 and 28
Phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo method in the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov manifold
abstract: We formulate and implement the phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) method in the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (HFB) manifold for systems with strong pairing correlations. Our formulation introduces a more flexible representation of HFB walkers with an explicit analytical expression for the normalization factor derived from the representation matrix with respect to the reference vacuum. We also extend our previously developed stochastic gauge formalism from the Slater determinant manifold to the HFB framework, providing additional flexibility for controlling stochastic fluctuations. Benchmark calculations for the Richardson model demonstrate the accuracy and numerical stability of the method.

title: Detecting Tidal Resonances in Binary Neutron Stars
abstract: As a binary neutron star inspirals due to the emission of gravitational waves, the rising tidal frequency resonantly excites vibrational modes. These oscillations are seismological probes of the rich stellar interior, yet it remains to be established whether gravitational-wave interferometers can measure them. Here, we present the first fully Bayesian study of the capability of the Einstein Telescope to detect tidal resonances. We simulate one year of observations and analyze the 200 loudest signals. We find that the Einstein Telescope can identify resonant modes and is sensitive to gravitational-wave phase shifts as small as Δ Φ ≈ 0.03 for favorable events. We further show that neglecting resonances can bias the inferred tidal deformabilities. These results establish tidal resonances as a measurable route for asteroseismology with future detectors.

title: Algebraic models of alpha-cluster nuclei
abstract: In this contribution I review the algebraic cluster model (ACM) for $\alpha$-conjugate nuclei with $A=4n$ and its extension to the cluster shell model (CSM) for $A=4n+x$ nuclei. The CSM describes the splitting of single-particles levels in a deformed field generated by the cluster of $\alpha$-particles. As an example, I discuss the energies, electromagnetic transitions and form factors of the neighboring nuclei $^{12}$C and $^{13}$C.

title: Feasibility of fast-alpha diagnostics with Pellet Charge Exchange
abstract: Characterization of fusion alpha particles is essential for the study of plasmas with significant alpha heating and, consequently, for the scientific success of ITER. Current diagnostic plans include gamma spectroscopy, collective Thomson scattering, charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, and a fast ion loss detector, although it remains unclear whether these methods will fully meet the requirements of this novel experiment. Pellet Charge Exchange (PCX) is an alternative approach in which alpha particles acquire electrons from the neutral cloud of an ablating fueling pellet through charge exchange, producing He+ ions and He atoms. The concept was previously tested in TFTR experiments, where escaping He atoms were analyzed using a neutral particle analyzer. In this work, a new optical approach is explored by modeling the emission of excited He+ ions produced in the charge exchange reactions. This signal could provide information on the density, energy, and distribution of fusion alpha particles along the pellet flight path, in the pedestal region of the plasma. The presented results are based on solving a system of rate equations for the n-resolved ionization states of alpha particles propagating through pellet clouds, with cloud parameters obtained from the Hydrogen Pellet Injection code HPI2. The model tracks the populations of ionization and excitation states of helium in one dimension, including the density of He+ (n = 4) states whose emission would be observed. Estimates of emission intensity and signal-to-background ratio based on expected bremsstrahlung radiation are also provided, identifying viable parameter ranges for PCX diagnostics.

title: Complex magnetism in a transition metal nitride
abstract: Abstract High-symmetry lattices of transition metal ions such as the body-centred tetragonal (bct) arrangement are model systems for correlated electron physics and frustrated magnetism. Transition metal oxides or halides with the bct K 2 NiF 4 -type structure are extensively studied and have ground states dominated by strong interactions within the square layers, but materials exemplifying other bct ground states are much rarer. Here we show that Ca 2 CoN 2 , from the underexplored class of transition metal nitrides, has one of the complex magnetic ground states predicted for the bct lattice lying close to a spin-liquid instability. Ca 2 CoN 2 has been synthesised at high pressure in a large-volume press, and has a Na 2 HgO 2 -type structure where weakening of intralayer superexchange interactions leads to frustration. Our magnetisation and neutron diffraction experiments reveal an incommensurate spin order below 54 K, consistent with a double- k spin density wave with propagation vectors ( k 00) and (0 k 0) where k = 0.57. This phase lies close to the predicted crossover (at k = 0.64–0.69) to a modulated spin liquid, which could be explored through further chemical tuning. This work demonstrates the potential of transition metal nitrides as magnetic model systems, alongside the much-studied oxides and halides, for exploring complex spin orders and associated quantum phases.
