title: Development and commissioning of a LaBr3:Ce, Sr-based collimated hard x-ray spectrometer for MAST-U
abstract: A new collimated hard x-ray (HXR) spectrometer has been developed and installed on the Mega Amp Spherical Tokamak Upgrade (MAST-U) to support future studies of runaway electron generation and provide a diagnostic capability to plasma-facing components monitoring. The diagnostic is based on an Sr-codoped LaBr3:Ce scintillator (2″ × 2″) coupled to a fast data acquisition system capable of recording raw scintillation waveforms in both pulse and continuous modes, allowing detailed reconstruction of individual events using algorithms for optimization of spectrometric parameters and pulse-shape discrimination. The detector was energy-calibrated up to 4.8 MeV using standard spectroscopy sources and a 66Ga radioisotope. Its performance was then evaluated at the MC40 cyclotron (University of Birmingham), demonstrating stable operation at 1.1 Mcps, with gain shifts of less than 4%. Following successful validation, the diagnostic was installed using an existing midplane line-of-sight configuration of the MAST-U, passing through both plasma-facing components and the central column region. A neutron flux map was simulated to estimate the radiation environment within the diagnostic field of view defined by a 15 cm diameter penetration through 1.5 m of concrete biological shielding acting as a collimator, together with an additional 10 cm polyethylene layer. Following installation, the collimated HXR diagnostic demonstrated reliable operation by recording gamma-ray events and hard x-ray bursts during both ohmic and neutral beam injection heated plasma discharges, confirming the successful commissioning of the diagnostic on MAST-U.

title: The Importance of Curium-250 to the $\gamma$-Ray Signature of $r$-Process Remnants
abstract: Identifying the astrophysical sites of the heavy rapid neutron-capture process ($r$-process) remains one of the most prominent unsolved problems in nuclear astrophysics. Emitted $\gamma$-rays from the decay of unstable nuclei have been identified as a potential observable marker on both prompt and delayed timescales which could provide conclusive evidence of the presence of $r$-process activity. In this work, we identify and discuss the importance of $^{250}$Cm to the $\gamma$-ray spectra of remnants, showing that the decay spectrum of $^{250}$Cm dominates the $\gamma$-ray spectra of $r$-process ejecta across a broad timescale ($\sim$ 2,000 - 20,000 years). We highlight the uncertain nature of this spectra: $^{250}$Cm may decay via $\alpha$-decay, $\beta$-decay, and spontaneous fission, but the decay branchings are not experimentally known, and each decay channel produces unique spectral lines which may be observable. We examine the potential for observation of the most prominent spectral signatures, finding that for conventional neutron star merger remnants, $\gamma$-ray lines will be detectable in current and future detectors only in the very near galaxy ($\sim$ 1 kpc), but other sites which could produce a larger ejecta mass may have greater observable distances. Our findings highlight the potential of actinide decay chains to indicate r-process nucleosynthesis and further underscore the necessity of measuring the nuclear properties that define their characteristic spectral signatures.

title: Simultaneous reconstruction of emission spectra and anode current dynamics in nanosecond x-ray tubes using attenuation curves
abstract: The accurate determination of emission spectra in nanosecond pulsed x-ray tubes is critical for advanced non-destructive testing, high-speed radiography, and dosimetry calculations. In this paper, we propose a novel computational–experimental approach: the basis-pulse decomposition method with kinematic regularization. Instead of reconstructing the spectrum as a set of independent energy bins, the proposed algorithm shifts the search space into the time domain. The integral spectrum is represented as a temporal superposition of instantaneous physical basis spectra, strictly calculated using the known transient voltage waveform, Kramers’ law, and models of anode self-absorption and window filtration. To stabilize the solution, we introduce a kinematic regularization operator that penalizes non-physical, instantaneous jumps in the discharge current. This method not only yields a highly accurate, noise-robust emission spectrum but simultaneously extracts the hidden temporal dynamics of the anode current It directly from a single integral attenuation curve.

title: Relativistic viscous hydrodynamics in the Density Frame for heavy-ion collisions
abstract: We present a numerical study of relativistic viscous hydrodynamics in the Density Frame for boost-invariant flows in 2+1 dimensions. The Density Frame is a formulation of relativistic viscous hydrodynamics that is first order in time, requires no auxiliary fields, and has no non-hydrodynamic modes; the only parameters are the shear and bulk viscosities and the equation of state. We formulate the numerical method in terms of a discrete analog of the dissipative function, which guarantees that the discrete equations produce entropy on all length scales and leads to a remarkably robust algorithm. We test the method against the exact solution of kinetic theory in the relaxation time approximation with Gubser symmetry. In making this comparison, we clarify how the kinetic solution matches onto hydrodynamics: we organize the solution by the opacity and show how the Bjorken attractor passes onto the Gubser solution order by order in gradients. We then replace the hydrodynamic engine of the MUSIC code with the Density Frame, and compare the two for IP-Glasma initial conditions in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. The Density Frame smooths sharp gradients more rapidly. The largest differences arise in the bulk-viscous sector, where the bulk pressure in the Density Frame responds instantaneously to the flow, while in the M\"uller-Israel-Stewart-based MUSIC it relaxes over a finite time. With shear viscosity alone, the multiplicity, mean transverse momentum, and elliptic flow of final-state hadrons from the two codes are very similar. The Density Frame is now ready for a complete Bayesian analysis of heavy-ion data.

title: Nuclear-geometry-tagging events in high-energy Ne--Ne collisions
abstract: Nucleon-nucleon interactions within atomic nuclei give rise to collective properties such as deformation and nuclear clustering. Ultrarelativistic nucleon-nucleon collisions offer a novel way to probe the many-body correlations of the incoming nuclei, as the nuclear structure is reflected in the initial geometry of the produced system. State-of-the-art low-energy nuclear theory calculations predict highly deformed $^{20}$Ne nuclei with a characteristic $\alpha$+$^{16}$O bowling-pin-like shape. Since such nuclei have recently been collided at the LHC, investigating methods to maximise the sensitivity to the nuclear structure is pertinent. In this paper, we investigate whether body--body and tip--tip configurations of $^{20}$Ne nuclei can be identified in Monte--Carlo Glauber simulations using geometry-sensitive observables: the eccentricity, $\varepsilon_2$, and the transverse compactness, $d_\perp$. The nuclear configurations are obtained from nuclear lattice effective field theory calculations within the framework of Nuclear Lattice Effective Field Theory (NLEFT) and $\textit{ab initio}$ Projected Generator Coordinate Method (PGCM). We utilise a Fisher linear discriminant to select body--body and tip--tip configurations based on the $\varepsilon_2$-$d_\perp$ correlation. With classifier thresholds chosen to retain $30\%$ of the target class in a validation sample, the two-variable Fisher selection obtains purities in NLEFT (PGCM) of $0.201$ ($0.156$) and $0.573$ ($0.540$) for body--body and tip--tip events, respectively.

title: Meson spectroscopy from lattice QCD
abstract: Determining the meson spectrum directly from Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) remains a central challenge, since QCD is strongly coupled at low energies and most excited states appear as resonances in hadronic decay channels. Advances in lattice QCD and scattering theory now provide a systematic framework for extracting meson spectra and resonance properties from first principles. Here I present an overview of this program and review current state-of-the-art calculations in meson spectroscopy from lattice QCD. I highlight recent progress in the extraction of resonant and coupled-channel amplitudes, along with frontier developments in three-body dynamics and the determination of meson photo-couplings. Together, these advances are bringing us closer to a comprehensive first-principles description of the excited meson spectrum.

title: Full-field and full-spectrum response efficiency calibration of x-ray grazing incidence microscope
abstract: Quantitative analysis of inertial confinement fusion (ICF) implosion hotspots requires accurate measurements of spatially distributed x-ray emission spectra. Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) x-ray microscopes are widely used for hotspot diagnostics in major ICF facilities; however, accurate calibration of their full-field and full-spectrum response efficiency remains challenging due to multi-parameter coupling and spatially nonuniform optical response. In this study, we present an efficient calibration method for a KB microscope by combining theoretical modeling with experimental reflectivity measurements. The response efficiency is described in terms of the collection solid angle, magnification, and angle-dependent mirror reflectivity, while experimental data are used to calibrate key model parameters, including the effective grazing incidence angle and a global intensity correction factor accounting for system-level losses. The method is applied to a four-channel, energy-adaptive KB microscope, enabling determination of the spatial distribution of the effective response energy and the full-spectrum response efficiency over the entire field of view. This approach provides a reliable basis for quantitative ICF hotspot imaging diagnostics.

title: Feasibility study of secondary-electron-bremsstrahlung imaging with a knife-edge slit camera for range verification in carbon-ion therapy
abstract: Abstract Secondary-electron-bremsstrahlung (SEB) imaging has been proposed as a method for in vivo range verification in particle therapy; however, insufficient detection sensitivity remains a major limitation, particularly under low-count conditions. In this study, we developed a knife-edge slit camera and evaluated its feasibility for carbon-ion beam range verification using one-dimensional SEB profiles. The camera consisted of a tungsten knife-edge slit collimator and a 16 × 16 Ce:GAGG scintillator array coupled to an 8 × 8 SiPM array. Experiments were performed at the Heavy Ion Medical Accelerator in Chiba using a 290 MeV/u carbon-ion beam irradiated onto a water phantom. One-dimensional SEB profiles were acquired for different beam ranges controlled by range shifters. The measured profiles shifted systematically with beam range. The profiles measured with range-shifter water-equivalent thicknesses of 0.00 and 5.27 mm were visually distinguishable. Calibration-based range estimation, evaluated by Poisson resampling of high-statistics measured profiles, yielded mean precisions of 2.76, 8.89, and 29.5 mm for 10 8 , 10 7 , and 10 6 incident carbon ions, respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility of knife-edge slit SEB imaging for carbon-ion beam range verification and indicate that further improvement in detection sensitivity is required for measurements with smaller numbers of incident ions.

title: Eccentricity as a Magnifying Glass: Precision Population Inference Enabled by Eccentric Neutron Star–Black Hole Mergers
abstract: Abstract The formation history of compact binary systems remains one of the key open questions in astrophysics. Theoretical studies generally favor isolated binary evolution for neutron star–black hole (NSBH) systems, which tends to produce nearly circular orbits. However, recent analyses of the gravitational-wave event GW200105 indicate that its source has measurable eccentricity, suggesting that alternative formation channels may also contribute. It has been shown that the intrinsic parameters of eccentric NSBH mergers, such as the component masses and spins, are much better measured than circular mergers with LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA (LVK) observatories. We explore how such eccentricity-enhanced parameter measurements can affect the inference of NSBH formation channels. We find that sharper measurements of the effective spin parameter χ eff increase the fraction of systems for which negative values can be confidently identified, allowing for the clear measurement of a spin–orbit misaligned event every ∼2.5 eccentric NSBH detections for an isotropically distributed population in the fifth LVK observing run (O5). Improved neutron star (NS) mass measurements provide better constraining power for NS mass distributions, potentially revealing structure and tightening the bounds that can be drawn on their upper and lower masses. Similarly, the recovery of a metallicity-dependent BH mass distribution is improved by eccentricity-enhanced measurements. Finally, we show that the proposed population-level eccentricity distribution for dynamical-formation channels can be tested by the end of O5.

title: Incorporating deep neural networks into lepton-nucleus interaction modeling
abstract: We present a scheme to incorporate precise inclusive cross-section predictions from a deep neural network trained on electron--carbon scattering data into a Monte Carlo event generator. The inclusive prediction is decomposed into independent exclusive interaction channels using the generator's theoretical models, and the resulting events are reweighted accordingly. We apply this scheme to investigate nuclear effects in inclusive and semi-exclusive electron-scattering measurements.

title: Coexistence of strange quark stars and neutron stars: Metastability and nucleation in protoneutron stars
abstract: If strange quark matter (SQM) is absolutely stable, hadronic neutron stars (NSs) and strange quark stars (QSs) may coexist in the so-called two-families scenario. A key issue is explaining how hadronic NSs can survive as long-lived metastable objects, rather than promptly converting into stable QSs. Since all NSs are born as hot proto-neutron stars (PNSs), a necessary condition for their existence is that the conditions for conversion, triggered by the nucleation of the first critical SQM droplet, are not reached in every PNS. We investigate the thermal nucleation of critical SQM droplets under representative PNS conditions, accounting for flavor-composition fluctuations and finite-size effects on color superconductivity by suppressing pairing in droplets smaller than the diquark coherence length. We define the nucleation conditions as the thermodynamic state at which a critical SQM droplet is expected to nucleate statistically within the characteristic dynamical timescale of the system. Under these conditions, the reduced nucleation barrier is nearly universal, with $W_*/T\simeq167$ to within a few units. Exploring the SQM parameter space, we show that requiring a canonical $1.4~\rm{M}_{\odot}$ NS to survive the PNS stage sets a lower bound on the hadron-quark surface tension $\sigma\gtrsim 67$ MeVfm$^{-2}$.

versions.title: Coexistence of strange quark stars and neutron stars: Metastability and nucleation in protoneutron stars
versions.abstract: If strange quark matter (SQM) is absolutely stable, hadronic neutron stars (NSs) and strange quark stars (QSs) may coexist in the so-called two-families scenario. A key issue is explaining how hadronic NSs can survive as long-lived metastable objects, rather than promptly converting into stable QSs. Since all NSs are born as hot proto-neutron stars (PNSs), a necessary condition for their existence is that the conditions for conversion, triggered by the nucleation of the first critical SQM droplet, are not reached in every PNS. We investigate the thermal nucleation of critical SQM droplets under representative PNS conditions, accounting for flavor-composition fluctuations and finite-size effects on color superconductivity by suppressing pairing in droplets smaller than the diquark coherence length. We define the nucleation conditions as the thermodynamic state at which a critical SQM droplet is expected to nucleate statistically within the characteristic dynamical timescale of the system. Under these conditions, the reduced nucleation barrier is nearly universal, with $W_*/T\simeq167$ to within a few units. Exploring the SQM parameter space, we show that requiring a canonical $1.4~\rm{M}_{\odot}$ NS to survive the PNS stage sets a lower bound on the hadron-quark surface tension $\sigma\gtrsim 67$ MeVfm$^{-2}$.

title: The Contribution of Disrupted Dense Star Clusters to Gaia’s Compact Object Binaries
abstract: Abstract We present the first model of the Milky Way’s detectable compact object–luminous star binary population from disrupted dense star clusters. We bridge large-scale cosmological star cluster formation with high-resolution dynamical evolution of compact object binaries by mapping the predicted star clusters from the EMP- Pathfinder simulations to N -body Cluster Monte Carlo models. We predict that approximately 3 × 10 5 white dwarfs (WDs), 1.5 × 10 5 black holes (BHs), and 1 × 10 3 neutron stars (NSs) in binaries with luminous companions are released to the Galaxy from now-disrupted dense star clusters throughout the history of the Milky Way. Synthetic observations modeled with the gaiamock pipeline reveal that the modeled Gaia DR3 yields are sparse (≈2 WDs, 0 NS, 0 BHs at 90% credibility), with the majority lying beyond the detection horizon. Gaia DR4 is expected to increase the observational yield of these systems only marginally, as the benefits of an expanded search volume are largely offset by the diminished astrometric and photometric precision of more distant sources (≈14 WDs, 0 NS, 0 BHs). While the underlying BH binary population is similar to that of WDs, they are detected far less frequently; they tend to pair with lower-mass, dimmer companions and have less temporal coverage of their long orbital periods. For NSs, we suggest that the observed overrepresentation of metal-poor, halo systems is inconsistent with an origin in disrupted dense star clusters. Instead, the observed Gaia NS population could reflect the accretion history of metal-poor, dwarf galaxies into the Milky Way, isolated binary star evolution, or supernova physics.

title: Proton femtoscopy in heavy-ion collisions: From transport theory to source imaging
abstract: Two-particle correlations play a pivotal role in understanding the space-time characteristics of particle emission in Heavy-Ion Collisions (HIC). A relative emission source typically represents these characteristics and can be obtained from transport model simulations such as the Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck (BUU) transport model. In this paper, we use the BUU transport model to simulate p-p sources while simultaneously using HIC correlation data to infer them for the same collisions, combining the Koonin-Pratt equation with Richardson-Lucy deblurring. In comparing the sources, we can isolate and provide a simple parametrization for source tails missing from BUU sources. These tails may be attributed to secondary decays that contribute at least one member of the pair in the source. With a tail added, the BUU can reproduce 80 MeV/u Ar + Sc and Ca + Ca measurements. We investigate the angular dependence of Ca + Ca correlations to infer the angle dependence of slow emissions. Our parametrization for the tail may be employed when no deblurring for source inference is pursued.

title: Neutrino mass predictions with metaheuristic optimization under $A_4$ modular symmetry
abstract: The current research aims to conduct an exhaustive investigation of the neutrino mass model based on $A_4$ discrete non-abelian modular symmetry, specifically in the context of the linear seesaw mechanism, where the conventional type I seesaw mechanism is extended, with particular attention given to the optimization of the parameters using incomprehensible but intelligible-in-time logics optimization algorithm (ILA), a metaheuristic optimization. Unlike other approaches to discrete flavor symmetry, the modular approach to flavor dynamics is found to significantly reduce the number and complexity of flavon fields required to give realistic textures to fermion masses. The key predictions include neutrino masses, $U_\text{PMNS}$ matrices, effective neutrino masses for neutrinoless double beta decay, beta decay, Dirac and Majorana CP violation phases for normal (NO) and inverted mass ordering (IO), offering testable implications. The working efficiency of the ILA optimization technique is also estimated. The optimized neutrino oscillation parameters are well consistent with recent experimental data. Our analysis also aligns with Planck cosmological constraints on the sum of neutrino masses $0.06<\Sigma m<0.12\ \text{eV}$.

title: Landau-Zener formula and resonant axion conversion in neutron star magnetospheres
abstract: We investigate the Landau-Zener description of resonant axion-photon conversion in neutron star magnetospheres. We find that this picture often fails for axion conversions to millimeter-to-optical band photons due to the characteristic resonance width exceeding the size of the conversion region. This comparison of scales yields a simple criterion for evaluating the validity of the Landau-Zener formula. We verify this criterion numerically, and show that when invalid, the Landau-Zener conversion probability may significantly deviate from the numerical result. In light of these findings, we revise constraints on axions from neutron star optical-band polarization searches.

title: GLOW. II. A Census of Oxygen in Low-mass Galaxies*
abstract: Abstract Oxygen is forged by stars and redistributed through galaxies by feedback-driven outflows, leaving a record of star formation and the baryon cycle imprinted on its present-day abundance and distribution. The Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds project quantifies the production, distribution, and retention of oxygen in 37 low-mass, low–metallicity, gas-rich galaxies in the nearby Universe ( D < 6 Mpc) spanning a critical stellar mass range (10 6.5 < M * < 10 9.5 ) where feedback is expected to strongly shape galaxy evolution. We incorporate literature results to extend the analysis over 10 5 < M * < 10 11.5 . We couple star formation histories derived from resolved stars with measurements of interstellar medium metallicity and gas mass, and compare the oxygen budgets with empirical constraints in the circumgalactic medium (CGM). We find low-mass galaxies retain between 4% and 25% (mean 11%) of their oxygen produced by stellar nucleosynthesis, and nearly all retained oxygen resides in the gas. Galaxies exhibit increased scatter to higher oxygen retention fractions when residing in denser environments (Θ 5 > 0.5) and within 1 Mpc of a massive galaxy ( M * > 10 9 M ⊙ ), indicating the environment likely affects the amount of oxygen retained, recycled, or accreted to galaxies. Contrary to expectations, oxygen retention does not correlate with position on the mass–metallicity relation. Although ionized oxygen is detected in the CGM, it remains unclear whether most missing oxygen resides there or has been expelled entirely. Hydrodynamical simulations, despite successfully reproducing the mass–metallicity relation, predict much higher retention fractions than measured in low-mass galaxies. Simple modeling indicates that wind mass-loading and outflow metallicity govern oxygen retention, and that low-mass galaxies accrete less baryonic material relative to the cosmic baryon fraction.

title: First Measurement of the Hubble Constant from Gravitational Wave–Galaxy Cross Correlations
abstract: Abstract We measure for the first time the Hubble constant ( H 0 ) from the cross correlation of galaxies and gravitational waves (GWs), by applying the Peak Sirens method. This method consists of finding the peak of the 3D angular cross-spectrum C ℓ ( z , D L ) between the galaxy redshifts ( z ) and the GW luminosity distances ( D L ). Using two GW events from the GWTC-3.0 catalog and the GLADE + galaxy catalog, we make the first detection of the cross-correlation peak at 5.9 σ confidence. This signal comes mostly from the best localized event in the catalog, GW190814, which alone provides a 3.4 σ significance. Adding the multimessenger event GW170817, but without using its known redshift, we find H 0 = 6 7 − 15 + 18 km s −1 Mpc −1 and the first observational constraint on the GW bias, b gw < 4.3 at 95% confidence interval. These measurements set the stage for future novel cosmological constraints with this technique.

title: Bayesian Inferences on the Twin-star Scenario from NICER Pulsars
abstract: Abstract We investigate dense-matter equations of state (EOSs) within a Bayesian framework, focusing on the constraints from the latest NICER mass–radius measurements of PSR J0614−3329 and the massive pulsar PSR J0740+6620, together with PSR J0030+0451 and PSR J0437−4715. For the hadronic sector, we adopt a meta-modeling EOS constrained by these NICER measurements. The hadronic inference indicates that PSR J0614−3329 favors a somewhat softer EOS than the other two ∼1.4 M ⊙ pulsars, while the ∼2 M ⊙ constraint prevents the EOS from becoming too soft. We then introduce a strong first-order phase transition through a constant-speed-of-sound quark-matter segment. Constraining the transition parameters with PSR J0614−3329 as the primary source and XTE J1814−338 as a secondary constraint, we find a preferred transition density of n t ∼ 3.3 n 0 , a sizable energy-density jump of Δ ϵ − Δ ϵ cr ∼ 800 MeV, and a relatively large posttransition sound speed of c s 2 / c 2 ∼ 0.7 . Including the additional constraint from HESS J1731−347 shifts these values to n t ∼ 2.7–2.8 n 0 , Δ ϵ − Δ ϵ cr ∼ 600–700 MeV and c s 2 / c 2 ∼ 0.85 . Such a phase transition generates a disconnected hybrid branch with radii of about 6–7 km at masses around 1.2–1.4 M ⊙ , and strongly suppresses the dimensionless tidal deformability relative to the purely hadronic branch. This pronounced change in tidal deformability is a characteristic signature of the twin-star mechanism and may provide an important observational tool for identifying phase transitions in neutron star matter in future multimessenger measurements. Our results demonstrate that the NICER data, particularly the recently measured PSR J0614−3329, when supplemented by XTE J1814−338, already provide meaningful constraints on both the strength of a first-order phase transition and the stiffness of the posttransition phase in dense matter.

title: Algal symbiosis adaptively restructures the cnidarian microbiome to enhance holobiont metabolism
abstract: Abstract Microbiomes are integral to the function and resilience of cnidarian holobionts, yet the spatial and functional integration of microbial communities within host tissues remains poorly understood. Here, we show that symbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellates induces adaptive, tissue-specific restructuring of the microbiome in the cnidarian model Aiptasia, fundamentally enhancing holobiont nitrogen assimilation and metabolic flexibility. Using laser microdissection, tissue-resolved metatranscriptomics, gnotobiotic hosts, and stable isotope tracing, we reveal that symbiosis profoundly restructures microbial communities across the epidermis and gastrodermis, enriching for taxa and pathways that support nitrogen assimilation in photosynthetically active tissues. Expression of microbial nitrite reductase is strongly upregulated in the symbiotic gastrodermis, and 15 N-tracer experiments demonstrate that bacterial assimilation of nitrite synergizes with algal symbionts to fuel the biosynthesis of essential amino acids. These findings show that symbiosis drives spatially compartmentalized microbiome adaptation within animal tissues, aligning microbial metabolism with host-algal nutrient exchanges to enhance holobiont functioning.

title: The role of spin polarization in event-by-event fluctuations
abstract: The event-by-event initial state fluctuations constitute a critical physical quantity for understanding the dynamics of high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Due to the extremely limited available experimental data of such fluctuations, it is difficult to constrain or direct the characterization of the underlying initial state properties. This work constrains the correlation function between the initial eccentricity and the asymmetry by employing a parton distribution function that incorporates spin polarization induced by thermal vorticity and thermal shear. Based on the kinetic theory calculations, we found that the asymmetry fluctuations considering spin polarization have a significant splitting effect compared to those without spin polarization. These splitting exhibit pronounced system size and energy dependence. Moreover, the ratios of correlation function display similar system size and energy dependence--particularly in the low-temperature regime ($T \lesssim$ 0.12 GeV). These results suggest that spin polarization may serve as a useful constraint method for the event-by-event initial state fluctuations of heavy-ion collisions.

title: A systematic study of hydrodynamic attractors in periodically driven systems at weak and strong couplings
abstract: We study equilibration and hydrodynamic response in conformal systems undergoing periodic expansion and contraction along one spatial direction. Using strongly coupled holography (AdS/CFT), weakly coupled kinetic theories (relaxation-time approximation, scalar $\phi^4$ theory and the Yang--Mills sector of QCD effective kinetic theory) and hydrodynamics (Navier--Stokes, M\"uller--Israel--Stewart (MIS) and rBRSSS), we investigate the shear response to a periodic drive of varying amplitude $A$ and frequency $\omega$, both analytically in linear response and numerically. We find that, at the linear level, $A\ll 1$, periodically driven systems approach a cyclic attractor that in general differs from Navier--Stokes behaviour. This attractor is universal among kinetic theories and accurately described by MIS theory: for slow driving, $\omega \tau_\pi \ll 1$, where $\tau_\pi$ is the shear relaxation time, it approaches the Navier--Stokes limit, whereas for fast driving the shear stress saturates at its non-interacting (free-streaming) value. In strongly coupled holographic systems, the periodic drive excites non-hydrodynamic quasinormal modes, which produce a characteristic ringing in the approach to the cyclic attractor, in contrast to the purely exponential approach found in kinetic theories. This difference is a direct consequence of the distinct non-hydrodynamic spectra of the two classes of theories. Moreover, unlike in kinetic theory, the holographic response is sensitive to the curvature terms of second-order hydrodynamics. Over longer times, non-linear viscous heating, which is quadratic in the drive amplitude, raises the temperature and thereby lowers $\omega\tau_\pi$, since $\tau_\pi\sim 1/T$. This induces a slow drift of the cyclic attractor, which eventually converges towards Navier--Stokes hydrodynamics at asymptotically late times.

title: Time evolution of the α -decay process in intense laser fields
Non-Efimovian two-neutron halos with an s − wave core-neutron resonance
Deep learning models for ADITYA-U MHD equilibrium
abstract: Abstract This work presents an integrated deep learning framework for rapid magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium estimation in the ADITYA-U tokamak. A free-boundary equilibrium database containing 100,760 cases was generated using the pyIPREQ Grad-Shafranov solver from experimentally derived operating conditions spanning 766 ADITYA-U plasma discharges, with constraints representative of circular limiter plasmas near the flat-top phase. The database was used to develop a cascaded framework for predicting scalar equilibrium quantities, 1d safety factor profiles, and 2d poloidal flux profiles. Dense neural networks, principal component analysis, convolutional neural networks and physics-informed neural networks were investigated within this framework. The error propagation, cross-models consistency and ablation study of Grad-Shafranov residual were performed for the proposed framework. Across the test dataset, the models achieve median mean absolute errors of 1e-2 for the safety factor profile and 2e-3 for the normalized poloidal flux profile. The largest model requires approximately 1 ms per equilibrium inference on a multi-core CPU. The results demonstrate the potential of the framework as a fast surrogate for equilibrium analysis, experiment planning and real-time plasma control applications for ADITYA-U experiments.

title: Soft X-Ray Detection Down to the Nitrogen K-Edge Using a Pixelated iLGAD Sensor
abstract: Hybrid pixel detectors represent the state-of-the-art technology for hard X-ray experiments at synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers, owing to their high frame rates, extended dynamic range, and scalable detection areas. However, their application in the soft X-ray regime remains bottlenecked by the challenge of developing a sensor that can achieve high quantum efficiency and an sufficient signal-to-noise ratio at low photon energies. Here, we present inverse low-gain avalanche diode (iLGAD) sensors integrated with a thin entrance window, demonstrating single-photon resolution down to 390 eV (below the Nitrogen K-edge) with a signal-to-noise ratio of 5. Two gain layer designs, standard gain layer and shallow gain layer, were systematically investigated to evaluate their spectral response as a function of photon energy and operating temperature. A double-peak feature is observed in the energy spectrum, arising from the dependence of charge multiplication on photon absorption depth. Furthermore, a phenomenological spectral fitting model was established, enabling the quantitative extraction of the effective $\mathrm{n}^+$ layer thickness and gain layer depth. Beyond providing a fundamental understanding of iLGAD charge multiplication mechanisms and characterization results in the soft X-ray regime, these findings lay the foundation for developing large-area, high-frame-rate hybrid pixel detectors for soft X-ray. This advancement directly benefits soft X-ray photon science applications, including high-resolution ptychography, spectroscopy, and resonant scattering at synchrotron and FEL beamlines.

title: Calorimetry as inference: the information content of particle showers and the limits of energy measurement
abstract: A calorimeter does not measure the energy of a particle, it infers it from the record the absorption process leaves behind. Energy conservation writes every event as an accounting ledger, E = E_dis + E_B + E_esc + E_nu, of which only the dissipated component contributes to signal, so resolution is limited by how well the record of the dissipation constrains the missing entries. We formalize this: records form a lattice on which information is monotone; thinning a Poisson record scales Fisher information exactly by the retention; clustered records read out as sums cost the 1/(1+cv^2); and the quadrature budget a/sqrt(E) (+) b is the floor of every summed readout. The "ultimate limits" of hadronic calorimetry are identified as the first rung of a ladder, the residual spread of the invisible energy around a single correlated observable. We measure the ladder above that rung on Geant4 truth records of hadronic showers in copper, from the dissipated-energy sum to time-, position- and multiplicity-resolved records, with estimators validated on exactly solvable toy models. The achieved full-record value, model-conditional, is about 5.5%/sqrt(E) (+) 0.3% over 20-100 GeV, a factor 1.7-1.9 below the canonical one-functional construction on the same events (1.29% vs. 2.14% at 20 GeV). Under retrained high-precision neutron transport it moves from 1.29% to 1.30%, the dissipated-energy sum by 7%, and the gain from time structure becomes 0.17% in place of 0.28%. Dual-readout supplies the largest share of the information. Shower shape is next, almost entirely longitudinal, saturating at about one interaction length. Time structure adds nearly as much with or without shower shape, and stopped-muon neutrino losses set an estimated floor of 0.99% at 20 GeV. Every readout dimension has a measured information exchange rate, separating what new hardware can buy from what better algorithms can recover.

title: Conceptual Design of a Compact Magnetic Spectrometer for Space Radiation Measurement
abstract: We present the design of COMIRA, a compact magnetic spectrometer for space radiation measurement. The spectrometer consists of four layers of scintillating fiber trackers, four layers of silicon strip trackers, one threshold Cherenkov counter, two anti-coincidence counters, and a permanent magnet. The detector has an overall dimension of approximately 12x12 cm3 and a geometrical acceptance of ~6.6 cm2sr. Based on combined measurements of charge, velocity, and rigidity (momentum/charge), it enables the simultaneous measurement of the energy spectrum, angular distribution and time evolution of individual radiation components, including electrons, positrons, protons and light nuclei over an energy range from tens of MeV to several GeV. The design can be further optimized depending on the available resources and constraints of the hosting space platform.

title: Precision tests of SM and new physics with the COHERENT Ge-mini and TEXONO data
abstract: A comprehensive numerical analysis of the latest germanium based coherent elastic neutrino nucleus scattering ( CE ν NS ) data from the COHERENT Ge-mini and TEXONO experiments has been conducted to test the Standard Model (SM) and search for new physics. By combining CE ν NS and E ν ES signals with a consistent treatment of detector effects and systematic uncertainties, we obtain a low energy determination of the weak mixing angle from COHERENT Ge-mini, in agreement with the SM prediction. We derive novel constraints on neutrino electromagnetic properties, including the magnetic moment, millicharge, charge radius, and anapole moment, with TEXONO providing particularly competitive bounds. Inclusion of E ν ES significantly improves the sensitivity to the neutrino millicharge by up to three orders of magnitude. We also investigated light scalar and vector mediators, finding striking complementarity between reactor and stopped pion sources across different mediator mass regimes. Finally, we put bounds on sterile neutral lepton production through transition dipole, scalar, and vector portals, probing masses from the sub-MeV to tens of MeV scale. Our results demonstrate that current germanium based CE ν NS experiments provide a powerful low energy laboratory for precision electroweak tests and complementary probes of a broad class of physics beyond the SM.

title: Magnetic scattering experiments with an ultrashort pulsed soft X-ray source using iLGADs
abstract: Inverse Low Gain Avalanche Diode (iLGAD) sensors developed at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in collaboration with the Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) have demonstrated an excellent Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Quantum Efficiency (QE) in the soft X-ray range. In the current batch, single-photon detection is achievable at 400 eV with an SNR > 5, while the QE surpasses 85 % at 250 eV. Combined with the high frame rates of CMOS readout ASIC, iLGAD sensors make the hybrid pixel detectors excellent candidates for time-resolved magnetic Small Angle X-ray Scattering (mSAXS) experiments in the soft X-ray energy range. In this contribution, we evaluated ILGAD sensors bump-bonded to 25 {\mu}m pitch charge-integrating M\"ONCH chips at a laser-driven soft X-ray source. During the experiments, we measured energy-dispersed radiation between 600 eV and 1500 eV. These measurements were performed for the iLGAD sensor, as well as for the standard silicon sensor. Using the high-precision electronic trigger of the X-ray source, we were able to synchronise the detector with the X-ray source delivering few-picosecond pulses and optimise the timing parameters for the acquisition. Finally, we successfully performed the mSAXS experiment probing the magnetic domain pattern of a FeGd heterostructure, demonstrating better performance than a M\"ONCH detector with a standard silicon sensor. ILGAD sensors achieved a significantly higher photon detection efficiency and, consequently, a higher sensitivity compared to standard silicon sensors under the same conditions, particularly for the lower-energy Fe L3 edge.

title: Machine Learning Sensor Fusion for Water Vapor Radiometry based Tropospheric Delay Calibration
abstract: The next-generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) intends to use 22 GHz water vapor radiometry (WVR) to correct for tropospheric phase fluctuations in its high-frequency bands. However, current delay-retrieval methods do not reach the required accuracy and reliability. As a remedy, we propose a machine-learning based retrieval concept and a preliminary architecture, framed as heterogeneous, multi-rate sensor fusion. Atmospheric reanalysis profiles and surface weather set the context in which per-antenna WVR spectra are used to estimate excess path by a Kalman filter whose parameters are learned from high-cadence calibrator phases. The method is being developed, with planned first validation on the 183 GHz WVR system of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).

title: High efficiency superconducting filterbank with impedance-defined resolution for millimeter-wave spectroscopy
abstract: We present a high efficiency, moderate resolution on-chip superconducting filterbank spectrometer designed for line intensity mapping and broadband wave-like dark matter searches. Existing implementations used by the millimeter-wave community rely on resistive feedline termination for standing wave mitigation which caps the per-channel efficiency $\eta_\mathrm{ch}$ at 50\% and utilize microstrip resonators which highly couple the resolving power $\mathcal{R}=\nu/\delta\nu$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}$ to thin-film dielectric loss. The architecture presented in this paper addresses these limitations by eliminating the termination resistor and employing niobium coplanar waveguide resonators patterned directly on single-crystal silicon, which fixes the resonator's internal quality factor by the silicon substrate property rather than by the loss tangent of a deposited film. The resolving power is set by the impedance ratio between the resonator and feedline. Electromagnetic and circuit simulations of a ten-channel filterbank near 90~GHz at unity oversampling show $\mathcal{R}=1170$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}> 78\%$, with no significant trend in efficiency across channels. A ten-channel prototype, designed for $\mathcal{R}=92\pm5$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}=(81\pm3)\%$ over 90--106~GHz with a 560~nm interlayer based on simulations, was fabricated and optically characterized, yielding $\mathcal{R}=208\pm74$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}=(77\pm6)\%$. Measured $\eta_\mathrm{ch}$ well above the 50\% termination limit, together with demonstrated impedance tuning of $\mathcal{R}$, validate the design principles of this filterbank spectrometer and establishes a route to high-efficiency, high-resolution on-chip spectrometer arrays.

title: Challenges in the verification of MOSAIX ASIC for ALICE ITS3
abstract: The MOSAIX is a wafer-scale, full-functionality prototype ASIC for the ALICE Inner Tracking System (ITS3) upgrade, implemented in $65\,\text{nm}$ stitching technology. It integrates 144 independently powered pixel matrices, eight $10\,\text{Gb/s}$ serializers, and on-chip data and power distribution, making full-chip verification highly resource-intensive (over $80\,\text{GB}$ of memory and 192,000 tests). Verification also targets a sophisticated power-up sequence and radiation conditions of $10^{6}$\ particles $s^{-1} cm^{-2}$ and $4\,\text{kGy}$ TID. This work presents a UVM-based verification strategy that identified 260 design errors and summarizes key lessons from ASIC sign-off.

title: Bayesian constraints on bosonic dark matter in neutron stars within a covariant density-functional equation-of-state ensemble
abstract: We investigate neutron stars admixed with repulsively self-interacting bosonic dark matter (DM) using current multi-messenger observations. The dark component is modeled as a complex scalar field coupled to baryonic matter only through gravity, allowing dark-core and dark-halo configurations. To quantify baryonic equation-of-state (EOS) uncertainties, we combine a three-dimensional scan over $(m_\chi,\lambda,F_\chi)$ with 27 DDME2-based covariant density-functional EOSs spanning $L_{\rm sym}=30,50,70$ MeV and $-600\le Q_{\rm sat}\le 1000$ MeV. The models are confronted in a Bayesian framework with NICER mass--radius measurements from the Amsterdam and Maryland/Illinois analyses and the GW170817 tidal-deformability constraint. After Bayesian evidence weighting over the EOS ensemble, the EOS-relevant dark-sector scale $\mu_\chi\equiv m_\chi/\lambda^{1/4}$ is localized around 250 MeV for both NICER data sets. In the $(m_\chi,\lambda)$ parameterization, the marginalized boson-mass posterior peaks at $m_\chi\simeq300$--$330$ MeV, while $\lambda$ remains broadly distributed. Since the bosonic EOS depends on $m_\chi$ and $\lambda$ only through $\mu_\chi$, their separate marginals are conditional on the adopted independent priors. The inferred DM fraction is more data-set dependent, with posterior modes near 4% for Maryland/Illinois and 12% for Amsterdam. Bosonic DM also shifts the inferred $Q_{\rm sat}$ from negative toward intermediate and positive values, whereas the response of $L_{\rm sym}$ is weaker. This indicates a model-dependent trade-off between DM-induced compactification and the high-density stiffness of baryonic matter. These constraints remain conditional on the selected EOS family and the assumption of a common effective $F_\chi$ for all sources.

versions.title: Bayesian constraints on bosonic dark matter in neutron stars within a covariant density-functional equation-of-state ensemble
versions.abstract: We investigate neutron stars admixed with repulsively self-interacting bosonic dark matter (DM) using current multi-messenger observations. The dark component is modeled as a complex scalar field coupled to baryonic matter only through gravity, allowing dark-core and dark-halo configurations. To quantify baryonic equation-of-state (EOS) uncertainties, we combine a three-dimensional scan over $(m_\chi,\lambda,F_\chi)$ with 27 DDME2-based covariant density-functional EOSs spanning $L_{\rm sym}=30,50,70$ MeV and $-600\le Q_{\rm sat}\le 1000$ MeV. The models are confronted in a Bayesian framework with NICER mass--radius measurements from the Amsterdam and Maryland/Illinois analyses and the GW170817 tidal-deformability constraint. After Bayesian evidence weighting over the EOS ensemble, the EOS-relevant dark-sector scale $\mu_\chi\equiv m_\chi/\lambda^{1/4}$ is localized around 250 MeV for both NICER data sets. In the $(m_\chi,\lambda)$ parameterization, the marginalized boson-mass posterior peaks at $m_\chi\simeq300$--$330$ MeV, while $\lambda$ remains broadly distributed. Since the bosonic EOS depends on $m_\chi$ and $\lambda$ only through $\mu_\chi$, their separate marginals are conditional on the adopted independent priors. The inferred DM fraction is more data-set dependent, with posterior modes near 4% for Maryland/Illinois and 12% for Amsterdam. Bosonic DM also shifts the inferred $Q_{\rm sat}$ from negative toward intermediate and positive values, whereas the response of $L_{\rm sym}$ is weaker. This indicates a model-dependent trade-off between DM-induced compactification and the high-density stiffness of baryonic matter. These constraints remain conditional on the selected EOS family and the assumption of a common effective $F_\chi$ for all sources.

title: Experimental demonstration of beam-driven wakefield acceleration in laser-plasma filament
abstract: Self-guided femtosecond laser pulses propagating in low-pressure gas can generate plasma filaments, establishing a framework for plasma wakefield acceleration (PWFA). This method exploits the intrinsic nonlinear light-matter interaction, reducing the energy required to generate plasma while enabling the realization of plasma stages suitable for PWFA. Here we report a proof-of-principle experimental demonstration of beam-driven wakefield acceleration of electron bunches with an accelerating field exceeding 250 MV/m in a laser-generated plasma filament. The witness bunch is accelerated while preserving both its charge and relative energy spread. The robustness and reproducibility of both the plasma source and the acceleration process are demonstrated with successful witness acceleration observed in 95% of the events and an rms energy jitter below 0.5%. The experimental observations are in agreement with particle-in-cell simulations, providing a consistent description of the underlying physical processes. These results demonstrate that laser-generated plasma filaments can serve as reliable plasma stages, delivering beam quality and operational reproducibility comparable to those achieved with established plasma-generation techniques. The concept bridges laser filamentation physics and compact accelerator technologies, offering a promising route toward sustainable, high-repetition-rate plasma-based facilities.

title: Searching for Ultra-Light Axions with Twisted Cavity Resonators of Anyon Rotational Symmetry with Bulk Modes of Non-Zero Helicity
abstract: M\"obius-ring resonators stem from a well-studied geometrical structure with a one-sided topology, the M\"obius strip, and have been shown to exhibit fermion rotational symmetry with respect to an untwisted ring resonator, which exhibits boson rotational symmetry [1]. Here, we present twisted hollow resonators with equilateral triangular cross-sections, leading to cavities with anyon rotational symmetry. Unlike conventional cavity resonators, these structures permit bulk resonant modes with a non-zero complex electromagnetic overlap $\mathcal C_p=\int_V\mathbf{E}_p\cdot\mathbf{B}_p^*\,d\tau$. The real and imaginary parts of this overlap couple to different observable quadratures. Although the negative-frequency component of a real axion field is immaterial for haloscopes employing a static DC magnetic field, it must be retained for a pumped resonator because the complex forms of Maxwell's equations differ for positive and negative frequencies and produce distinct upper and lower mixing branches. Retaining both branches shows that the real overlap produces amplitude-modulated sidebands, whereas the imaginary helicity of the modes studied here produces phase-modulated sidebands through the axion-photon chiral anomaly. A sensitive ultra-light dark-matter experiment may therefore be realised with an ultra-stable oscillator and a phase-sensitive readout. The sensitivity curves calculated here require the assumed noise floor to be interpreted as phase-modulation noise rather than amplitude-modulation noise, and consequently require sufficiently low residual oscillator phase noise at the axion Fourier frequency. The scheme removes the usual requirement for an external magnetic field and permits superconducting resonators with reduced surface loss and enhanced axion sensitivity.

title: Photon Calibration Techniques for High Resolution Cryogenic Detectors
abstract: Monoenergetic photons from a pulsed laser diode or LED are commonly used to calibrate the detector response of high-resolution calorimetric detectors. However, when the detector's resolution is larger than the energy of a single photon, a calibration is normally derived using Poisson statistics. In this paper, we clarify the assumptions implicit in this calibration method, before considering how a more realistic model of a detector's performance will violate these assumptions, biasing the calibration. Finally, we judge the individual impact of specific detector parameters on our calibration, and conclude with discussion of both the limits of our calculations and the implications for state-of-the art detectors.

title: Nucleon Wave Functions from QCD Vacuum Topology
abstract: Instantons, as topologically nontrivial gauge field configurations, provide a microscopic mechanism for chiral symmetry breaking and the $U_A(1)$ anomaly in QCD. Within the instanton liquid model (ILM), instantons generate multi-fermion interactions governed by their density and size. Using this framework, we develop a microscopic description of the nucleon based on instanton-induced quark--quark correlations. We derive the diquark interaction kernels arising from single instantons and instanton--anti-instanton molecules, revealing a strong attraction in the scalar channel and weaker correlations in the spin-one channels. Embedding these interactions in a covariant, permutation-symmetric Bethe--Salpeter--Faddeev equation yields a nucleon mass $m_N=939.53~{\rm MeV}$, with a predominantly scalar-diquark component ($98\%$) and a small axial-vector admixture ($2\%$) around the mass pole. Despite its small weight, the small admixture generates substantial spin--isospin interference, yielding an axial charge $g_A=1.265$, close to experiment. The resulting covariant amplitude is analytically continued to the light front to obtain the leading three-quark wave function. The corresponding unpolarized, helicity, and transversity parton distributions, along with their QCD-evolved moments, provide a direct connection to lattice QCD calculations and global-fit analyses. Our results show that the topology of the QCD vacuum organizes not only the nucleon mass and spin structure, but also its leading valence partonic content, providing a microscopic foundation for a more complete description including confinement and higher Fock components.

title: Non-contact temperature sensing and optical scatter in cryogenically-cooled crystalline silicon
abstract: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next generation gravitational-wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss (a driver of thermal noise), high thermal conductivity and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. In this paper, we report on the design and results of an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method relying on interference (optical fringes) made from reflections between the front and back surfaces. We also propose a scheme for implementation of this technique for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager. Additionally, we characterize the optical scattering of the sample in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures by using a high-sensitivity infrared camera. We measured relatively constant scatter with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of $(4.43\pm0.2)\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{sr^{-1}}$ at a scattering angle of $\theta_{s} = 7.5^\circ$ over the (cold-plate) temperature range of 123-294 K and saw no evidence for growth of cryogenic molecular layers (ice) on the sample in our current setup.

title: Magnetic Johnson noise from arbitrarily shaped conductors: experimental validation of the fluctuation-dissipation finite-element method
abstract: Magnetic Johnson noise--magnetic noise caused by thermal current fluctuations in conducting materials--can interfere with measurements and limit their sensitivity. As the sensitivity of experiments increases, it becomes increasingly important to accurately estimate the magnetic Johnson noise from experimental components with complex shapes during both the design and analysis phases. A particularly powerful approach is to combine the fluctuation-dissipation theorem with finite-element calculations. This versatile approach can be used to calculate the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors of arbitrary geometry for a wide range of frequencies and for magnetic field detectors with general geometries, such as a finite-sized loop or a gradiometer. Using a SQUID gradiometer array, we measured the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors with complex geometries and compared the results with calculations performed using this method. The calculations reproduce both the measured noise amplitude and its frequency dependence, providing an experimental validation of this method. We also performed a detailed analysis of how the geometry and material parameters affect the frequency dependence of magnetic Johnson noise.

title: Construction and Commissioning of a Compact Xenon Gas Recycling System for a High-Harmonic Generation VUV Frequency Comb
abstract: A compact, closed-loop xenon recycling system for application in a High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) Vacuum-UV (VUV) frequency comb laser systems is designed, constructed and commissioned. It consists of three main sections, a low-pressure section (LPS) pre-filtering the gas of particulates, water and hydrocarbons, then a compression station (CS), allowing for a variable pressure of up to 60 bar, and a high-pressure section (HPS) with more filtering, pressure control and monitoring. The system proves to meet all design criteria in gas quality (the sum off all hydrocarbon contaminations up to 120 amu and CO$_{2}$ being below 10$^{-8}$ mbar) and recovery efficiency (>99.8$\%$ for all expected operational cases, neglecting possible geometric gas catcher losses in the HHG laser itself). The operation and results are presented and discussed. Furthermore, the system is compared to the performance of a similar system from which it is derived.

title: Complex potential and the thermal width of quarkonium in quark-gluon plasma
abstract: We study the complex heavy quark anti-quark potential in lattice 2+1 flavor QCD at non-zero temperature. We point out a close relation between the imaginary part of the potential and the thermal quarkonium width. Using this relation, we estimate the thermal width of charmonia and bottomonia at high temperatures, which are not yet accessible with direct lattice QCD calculations of the quarkonium correlation functions and compare these to the results of the T-matrix analysis. For some of the excited quarkonia states, our estimates of the thermal width are smaller than the ones obtained in the T-matrix analysis.

title: An Assessment of Water Vapor Radiometry Landscape in ngVLA Context
abstract: The ngVLA intends to utilize Water Vapor Radiometry (WVR) as an approach to lower calibration overheads for tropospheric phase fluctuation correction in its high frequency bands (5 \& 6; 30.5-116 GHz) to levels below those feasible with fast switched reference gain calibration. As a stepping stone to an eventual ngVLA WVR system, the JVLA/ngVLA teams pursued an effort to develop and install a set of MMIC based compact water vapor radiometers (CWVR) and carry out on-sky testing. Most recent tests found that the CWVRs installed on the VLA antennas under this effort were non-functional in tracking visibility phases. As part of the program to develop a WVR system for the ngVLA, this memo summarizes the current landscape of water vapor radiometry experience, the situation with the CWVRs, how they relate to the ngVLA WVR requirements, and the work needed to operationalize the CWVRs as useful test systems and to make broader progress. We currently lack statistically relevant WVR correction data to understand their expected performance for the ngVLA sites. We also discuss parallel additional approaches alternative and/or complementary to the CWVRs. A path involving tests to establish the functionality, stability, sensitivity, and switched power cal/data synchronism of the CWVR system in the lab and on antenna, followed by on-sky tests, and a parallel effort to assess the utility of autocorrelation outputs of the VLA K-band receivers for delay estimation is recommended. Potential paths going beyond traditional excess path estimation methods which may be necessary to meet ngVLA requirements and goals are touched upon.

title: Playing CHESS with stars. II. Homogeneous analysis of high-resolution optical spectra for a sample of 135 giants in 14 bulge globular clusters
abstract: Bulge globular clusters are key tracers of the complex formation history of the Galactic bulge, as they retain information on its past star-formation episodes. Their chemical abundances serve as empirical “fossil records” of the early evolution of the bulge. We present a homogeneous analysis of archival high-resolution UVES spectra for 135 giants in 14 Galactic bulge globular clusters. We explore the results in the context of the phenomenon of multiple stellar populations and discuss what the abundances reveal about the chemical evolution of the bulge. We employed the CHEmical Survey analysis System (CHESS) pipeline to derive atmospheric parameters on an accurate scale defined by reference stars. Abundances for Li, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Sc, Y, Zr, Ba, Ce, Nd, and Eu were derived by spectrum synthesis. Deviations from local thermodynamic equilibrium (i.e., non-LTE or NLTE) were taken into account for Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Y, Ba, and Eu. We serendipitously discovered a Li-rich giant with A(Li) = 1.68 (after 3D NLTE corrections) in NGC 6723, which was hidden in the archival data. Our sample includes both first- and second-generation stars, as indicated by the observed spread in Na abundances. Compared to halo clusters, the bulge clusters show a lower α/Fe plateau at low metallicity and a more gradual decline in α/Fe toward higher metallicities. The Sc abundances are below solar and lower than in disk stars of the same metallicity. This difference could be important for solving open questions about the nucleosynthesis of this element. None of the clusters exhibit any significant spreads in heavy elements. Most clusters exhibit Ba/Eu ∼ 0.0, indicating a contribution from both s- and r-processes. Clusters with Fe/H $<$ -0.5 show negative Ce/Nd ratios, supporting the idea that these elements were predominantly produced by the r-process in these clusters.
